The 3-day AI RevOps operating system

Build a Funnel That Turns Strangers Into Retained Customers — In 3 Days.

This is the exact system we use to take someone who's never heard of you and walk them all the way to money in the bank — and then keep them paying month after month.

Here's the deal: most people build funnels backwards. They obsess over the logo, the colors, the "perfect" landing page — and never stop to ask the only question that matters: what has to be true for a stranger to pay me?

Over the next 3 days, you'll answer that question with a real, working funnel. Not theory. Not a course you'll never finish. An actual engine — pages, templates, automations, and an AI orchestrator — that runs while you sleep.

◆ What you'll walk away with

A complete AI RevOps engine: a strategy on one page, a conversion engine that feeds every asset, all your funnel pages and templates, an AI orchestrator running the operations, and the unit-economics to scale it to $1M ARR.

FoundationsThe Thing You're Actually Building

What Is AI RevOps?

RevOps is one word for something most companies run as two departments — and the gap between those two departments is where most revenue quietly dies.

Marketing owns the top. The ads, the content, the posts, the emails you send, the messages you send, the billboard, the spot on TV. Sales owns the bottom. The call, the demo, the proposal, the close. Between them sits a handoff: marketing counts leads, sales counts deals, and nobody owns the distance in between. Ask both teams why a quarter missed and you'll get two confident answers that don't touch each other.

Revenue operations is the decision to stop running it as two jobs. One system, one owner, one set of numbers — from the first second a total stranger sees your name, to the moment money clears your bank account.

Trace the whole thing once and it stops feeling abstract. Someone who has never heard of you sees something: an ad in a feed, a founder's post, a cold email, a message, a billboard on a commute, thirty seconds on TV. That touch has exactly one job — be seen by the right person. They click. They land somewhere. They hand over an email or a number, or they don't. They get a sequence. They turn up to something: a page, a session, a call. They're qualified, or they aren't. They see an offer. They buy. The payment settles. They get onboarded — and then they either stay or they leave.

Cold stranger to cleared payment — one system, not two departments
Read the top row as a set of numbers, not a story. Seven stages, seven counts, six rates between them. The moment you own all of them you stop arguing about whose fault a bad quarter was.

Here's the part that's actually new. Those four layers — touchpoints, people, data, plumbing — have always existed. Every company has had them, in some state, forever. What changed is that all four are now addressable by software that can reason. An agent can read the CRM, write the sequence, watch the step rates, spot which one dropped, draft the fix and schedule the send. Not because the model is magic, but because each layer already exposes an API and something can finally hold all of them at once.

◆ So what does the "AI" in AI RevOps actually mean

Not a chatbot bolted onto a website. It means the operator of the system is an agent rather than a person with twelve browser tabs open. You still decide the strategy, the offer and what ships. The agent does the reading, the writing, the wiring and the measuring — the work that was previously split across a marketer, an ops person and a sales manager who each saw a third of the picture.

◆ Where you'll be by Friday

You'll have the knowledge, the tools, the prompts, the workflows and the automations to stand this entire system up on your own — cold stranger to cleared payment, instrumented end to end, with an agent operating it.

FoundationsWhy This Shape, and Not Just a Better Product

Why Do You Need a Funnel — A Conversion Engine?

Here's the deal: people buy on a promise and stay on a result. Those are two different forces, and almost every funnel ever built addresses only the first one.

You can be genuinely excellent at earning the yes and still lose the customer — because nothing you built does anything about the gap between the moment they pay and the moment the thing actually works for them. That gap is where churn lives. It is also, almost always, invisible on the dashboard that told you the campaign was a success.

So a conversion engine is not a machine for getting a yes. It's a machine for delivering value continuously — before the sale, to earn the yes, and after it, to make the yes hold.

Excitement peaks at purchase. Value arrives later. The gap is the churn window.

Why the Sale Alone Doesn't Hold It

Software is supposed to be stickier than a course. It isn't — not on its own. Russell Brunson puts the mechanism precisely, crediting it to Bill Glazer: what he calls the pain of disconnect is not a property of the software at all. It's a property of what the customer has built inside it. Someone who never deployed anything churns exactly like a course they never opened. What creates the switching cost is usage — and what creates usage is being taught.

Alex Hormozi's SaaS case study is the cleanest version of this. His team replaced a 25-person group onboarding call with a one-to-one session that restated the customer's own goal, delivered a single quick win, and booked the next meeting from inside that meeting so nobody was left in no-man's-land. Ascension to the next offer went from 20% to 48%. His principle is worth writing down: the best way to get someone to expect value in the future is to give them value today.

Dan Martell's version is blunter. His own company ran 12% monthly churn — a nine-month customer. A client of his went from 18% to 4% monthly by building an on-ramp (teach the movements before the first class), a peer community so people feel part of something rather than merely using a tool, visible case studies, and a member-at-risk monitor.

Four different mechanisms — they need four different assets

Why Every Brand You Can Name Already Does This

Look at any well-known software or service brand and you will find the same set of things, without exception. They publish content continuously. They run webinars and live sessions. They write books. They run workshops and events. They host a community.

None of that is charity and none of it is "brand awareness." Every one of those is a carefully built conversion engine — a mechanism that takes someone cold, gives them something genuinely useful, and moves them one step closer to buying. And then keeps running after they've bought, because staying on top of mind is what turns a customer into a member of a tribe. The same asset does two jobs depending on which side of the sale the reader is standing on.

The same five assets, working both sides of the sale
You are not building five things. You're building five wrappers around one engine — and each one keeps earning after the sale, which is the half almost everybody skips.
On the numbers people quote here. A Forrester Consulting study commissioned by Intellum (2024, 300 director-level-and-above decision-makers) reported roughly 22% higher product retention, 38.3% higher adoption and 35% higher lifetime value per trainee. Treat those as directional, not proof: the study was commissioned by a customer-education vendor and the figures are self-reported by the people who run those programmes. A TSIA survey of about 2,800 customers found 68% say they use the product more after training — that is perceived behaviour, not measured usage. TSIA itself notes only 11% of firms have ever analysed whether content consumption actually affects renewal. Use them to argue direction; never as a promised result.
◆ The honest limit — read this before you over-build tutorials

Results alone plateau. Brunson's own position in Expert Secrets is that if the only thing you ever do is help someone achieve a result, they will eventually leave you anyway. Enablement gets them to the result. Community and a visible next rung are what keep them past it. Build both, or you'll do all this work and still watch people go quiet at month nine.

◆ What this means for the next three days

Every page, sequence and automation you build is in service of one thing: moving the value crossing earlier and then continuing to deliver value on the far side of the sale. If a thing you're about to build does neither, it's decoration — cut it.

FoundationsThree Shapes, Every Stage, Every Tool

What Are Funnels?

A funnel is the path a stranger walks to become a paying customer — and then a returning one. Every funnel has the same jobs: get attention, capture it, keep it warm, convert it, get paid, and keep them. What changes is the shape: the moment and the format in which you ask.

These are the three shapes this programme builds in depth, each played as the same machine you saw on the masterclass page: every stage of the Tantra Pro Funnel and Tantra Pro Flow, the tools that run it and the maths between stages, then the AI engine and the finished system. FoundationsRead This First

The Big Picture: One System, Three Shapes

Strip away the jargon and every funnel on earth — a live workshop, a quiz, a video sales letter, an Amazon product page — does the same four things in the same order. What changes is the shape, not the system.

The Daily Rhythm: Watch → Fill → Get → Do

Every day of the workshop runs the same four beats.

1 · Watch
The Live SessionTeaching plus Q&A, live. No recording-only days — you're building alongside everyone else.
2 · Fill
The Survey, in ParallelA full-screen form open next to the session. Every question has sample answers so you always know what "good" looks like.
3 · Get
Your Generated OutputYour answers run through an AI workflow and come back as a PDF plus a live link — by WhatsApp and email, same day.
4 · Do
The Short HomeworkOne small task that unblocks tomorrow. Skipping it is the single biggest reason people fall behind.
A note on the numbers. The figures in the diagrams are working teaching models, not client results. They come from a reference funnel spec and exist to show you the shape of a healthy funnel and the arithmetic that connects the stages. Your numbers will differ. The whole point of Day 3 is that you fetch your own.

Every Funnel Has 4 Jobs

Traffic, capture, convert, retain. That's it. Every tool, page and automation you will build this week exists to do one of those four things — and the reason funnels beat "post and pray" is that you can see which of the four is broken.

The funnel as one system — traffic in, retention out
Read it as a diagnostic: the sharpest narrowing (−92% from lead to buyer) is where the funnel leaks — so that's where nurture and the conversion engine earn their keep. The teal loop is why retention compounds.

The Whole Machine, on One Page

Those four jobs get delivered by six stages. This is the master map — the thing you'll be building for the rest of the week. Print it. Everything in Days 1–5 is a zoom-in on one of these bands.

The 6-stage funnel system — traffic in, retained revenue out
Read it top to bottom once, then bottom to top. Top-down is how a stranger travels. Bottom-up is how the money travels: S6 keeps them, S5 books them, S3 shows them up, S2 captures them, S1 finds them. Figures are teaching models, not client results.
◆ Why six stages and not four

The four jobs are the theory. The six stages are the build. "Capture" sounds like one thing until you realise a landing page (S2) and a show-up sequence (S3) are entirely different assets with entirely different failure modes — and that a funnel with a great page and no nurture loses more than half its registrations before the event even starts.

One Funnel, Three Shapes

You're not all building the same funnel. Some of you need a live webinar. Some need a multi-day workshop. Some need a reverse squeeze page that gives value before it asks for anything. Same six stages. Different shape at each one.

The same six stages, expressed three ways
Notice what never changes: five channels in, a capture moment, a show-up mechanism, a delivery moment, a close, and a loop. The shape is a choice. The system is not.
◆ And the other 17 types?
They're RecombinationsA product launch is a webinar funnel stretched over four videos. A book funnel is a reverse squeeze where Part 1 is 200 pages. A challenge is a webinar that refuses to end.
Same Six StagesEvery one of the 20 types in the library maps onto S1–S6. What differs is which stage carries the weight — and how many hours it costs you to build.
You Pick Yours on Day 1All 20 are laid out grouped by the job they do, with a build-hour estimate attached to each — so the choice is made against real cost, not vibes.

Where Your Offers Live: The Value Ladder

Before you pick a funnel type, you need to know what the funnel is selling into. Almost nobody buys the expensive thing first. They buy a small thing, it works, and they climb.

Here's the deal: a funnel isn't a machine for selling one product. It's a machine for moving someone up a ladder. And the ladder has a shape — each rung asks for more commitment and returns more value, while the crowd on each rung gets smaller.

The value ladder — commitment rises, audience narrows, value compounds
The load-bearing rung is the entry offer. Price it so the revenue it produces covers the cost of the traffic that produced it, and your top of funnel becomes free — every rung above it is then pure margin.
◆ Example · this workshop's own ladder

You're standing on one right now. Free content brought you here. The 3-Day AI RevOps Workshop is the entry offer — deliberately priced to cover the cost of filling it. Inside it you get a month of the app included. Above it sits a core program (course, community, group coaching) and above that a flagship tier (long-horizon access plus one-to-one implementation). Five rungs, one system, and each rung sells the next by working.

◆ Pro tip · build the ladder before the funnel

If you only have one thing to sell, your funnel has to do all the persuading in one shot — and your traffic has to be profitable on the very first transaction. That's the hardest game in marketing. Two rungs is dramatically easier than one. If you don't have a second rung yet, write one down today; you'll need it by Day 3.

Most businesses are great at one of these and terrible at the rest. A "viral" post with no capture step leaks every visitor. A beautiful sales page with no traffic is a billboard in the desert. The funnel's job is to make all four work together.

◆ Why retention is the whole game

Acquiring a customer costs money. Keeping one costs almost nothing. That's why the north star of this entire system isn't the first sale — it's MRR: recurring revenue that compounds month after month. Everything before it exists to earn Day 3's retention.

The One Equation to Memorize

You don't need an MBA. You need this:

The funnel equation

Profit = (Traffic × Conversion rate × Price) − Cost to deliver

Pull any one lever up and profit moves. The magic is that you can pull all four — and a funnel is just the machine that lets you pull them on purpose instead of by accident.

That's the version you can hold in your head. But it has a flaw: "conversion rate" is a guess. On Day 1 you'll replace every symbol in that equation with a number your funnel actually reports — a counted event with a named source — and by Day 3 you'll be reading those numbers weekly and fixing whichever one is lowest.

◆ The rule that runs through the whole week

Never model your funnel with invented rates. Every step you build gets instrumented as an event. The count of that event is the metric. A "conversion rate" is just one count divided by another. If you can't fetch it, you can't fix it — and you'll be optimising by vibes.

Day 1Strategize · The Offer, the Audience and the Engine

Decide What You Sell, and Exactly Who You Sell It To

Day 1 uses zero tools and decides 90% of the outcome. Everything you build on Days 2 and 3 is generated from today's answers — so a vague answer today becomes a vague landing page on Wednesday and a dead campaign next month.

Funnel vs. Random Marketing

Random marketing is post-and-pray. You publish, you boost, you hope. A funnel is different: every step has one job, and each step earns the next. If a visitor doesn't take the next action, that step is broken — and you know exactly which one.

◆ The mindset shift

If a customer doesn't understand or use what you sell, that's not their fault — it's yours. Your funnel owns the whole journey, from "who are you?" to "I can't run my business without this." Own the whole journey and retention stops being a department.

The Three Questions Every Funnel Answers

  1. Who is this for? Specific enough that the right person reads it and thinks this is me — and the wrong person leaves without wasting your money.
  2. What transformation do they get? Nobody buys a tool. They buy the after-state: the version of their business that exists once the problem is gone.
  3. Why now, and why you? The mechanism. The reason your way works when everything they've already tried hasn't.

The rest of this half is just answering those three properly. Question one is your ICP. Question two and three are your offer. Then you pick the funnel shape that carries them, and you write down the arithmetic that says whether it can work.

Step 1 — Define Who You're Actually For

Here's the deal: "small businesses" is not an audience. It's a way of avoiding a decision. A usable definition has two halves — the account you're selling to, and the person inside it who signs. Most people write the second and skip the first, then wonder why their outreach lists are garbage.

From a whole market to one winnable account — then to one person
Both halves or neither. The account definition tells you where to find them — it's what you type into a list-building filter. The persona tells you what to say — it's what your copy is written to.

The Ten Fields. Fill Every One.

Write an actual value in each row. If you can't, that's not a formatting problem — it's the thing you have to go find out.

#FieldWhat "good" looks likeWhere the answer comes from
1Headcount band"11–50 employees" — not "SMB"Your own closed-won list
2Revenue bandThe floor below which they cannot afford the outcomeEnrichment data · their own site
3IndustryOne to three. "All B2B" means you'll write to nobodyYour best 20 customers
4GeographyWhere you can actually deliver and get paidYour last 20 deals
5Role & seniorityOwner or decision-maker — someone who can say yes aloneWho signed, on the deals you won
6Their goalThe number they are measured on, in their wordsAsk ten of them. Not a guess
7Their challengeWhat's blocking that number right nowThe same ten
8Where they get informationNamed publications, communities, peopleAsk — then go and be there
9Buying processWho else signs, typical cycle length, usual blockerYour lost deals, honestly reviewed
10The triggerThe event that makes this urgent this quarterFunding · a new hire · a launch · a rule change
Fields 1–4 are what you paste into a list-building filter; 5–9 are what your copy is written to; field 10 is the one almost everyone skips and the one that decides your timing.
Task 1.1Find the Pattern in Your Best Customers

Don't invent an ICP. Extract one. Pull your 20 best accounts — best by revenue, retention and how easy they were to serve, not just revenue — and look for what they share across fields 1–4.

  1. List the 20 in a sheet, one row each.
  2. Add a column per firmographic field and fill it from data you already have.
  3. Find the values that appear in more than half the rows. That's your starting profile.
  4. Now look at your worst five accounts and write down what they share. That's your first negative criterion.
OwnerYouToolSpreadsheet or your CRMTime45 minDeliverableICP one-pager, fields 1–4ProofEvery value traced to a real account, not an opinion
Task 1.2Write the Person, and the Objection

Fields 5–9. If you've spoken to ten customers this year you can write these from memory. If you haven't, send five messages before tomorrow's session — one question each: "what number are you personally judged on this quarter, and what's in the way?"

Field 9's answer must include the sentence that kills your deals. Write it verbatim. You'll be answering it on every page you build on Day 2.

OwnerYouToolNone — or five DMsTime30 minDeliverablePersona card, fields 5–9ProofThe objection is quoted, not paraphrased
◆ What changes per funnel type · the ICP
Webinar FunnelYour ICP has to be list-addressable — you must be able to build a searchable list of them, because you'll be inviting named people to a dated event.
Workshop · ChallengeAdd one field: can they show up three days running? A cohort demands repeated attention, which rules out audiences that are structurally too busy.
Reverse SqueezeYour ICP must be content-reachable. You're leading with value to strangers, so you need a place they already gather — a feed, a community, a search term.
Other types: a book funnel needs an audience that still reads long-form · free-plus-shipping needs a shipping address you can serve · a JV funnel doesn't need an ICP you can reach at all — it needs a partner who already reaches them.

Step 2 — Design the Offer

An offer is not a price list. It's an argument: this outcome, by this method, in this time, and here's who carries the risk if it doesn't work. There's a clean way to pressure-test that argument before you spend a rupee or a dollar on traffic.

Pressure-test the value, then stack the offer
Run the equation before you write a word of copy. If the value isn't there, no headline saves it — and if it is, the headline almost writes itself out of the numerator.
◆ Pro tip · sell the transformation, not the tool

"Omnichannel outreach software" is a yawn. "Never wonder where your next ten clients are coming from" is a sale. Same product, completely different funnel. The tool belongs in the mechanism line, never the headline.

Task 1.3Score Your Offer on All Four Levers

Four rows, honest scores out of 10, and — this is the part people skip — one specific change written next to each.

  • Dream outcome — is it a number and a deadline, or an adjective?
  • Perceived likelihood — what proof does a sceptic see in the first ten seconds?
  • Time delay — what could they achieve in week one? If the answer is "nothing," build a week-one win.
  • Effort & sacrifice — which step could you do for them instead of teaching them to do it?

Fix your two lowest scores first. Ignore the rest for now.

OwnerYouToolNoneTime30 minDeliverableScored offer + two committed changesProofEach lever has a concrete change, not a score alone
Task 1.4Write the One-Sentence Offer, Then Place It on the Ladder

Fill the template from the diagram. Then read it out loud to someone who doesn't know your business. If they have to ask a follow-up question, it isn't done.

Then place it: which rung is this — entry, core, or flagship? And name the rung above it, even if you haven't built that yet. A ladder with one rung forces your traffic to be profitable on the first transaction, which is the hardest game there is.

OwnerYouToolNoneTime20 minDeliverableOffer sentence + ladder positionProofAt least two rungs named and priced
◆ What changes per funnel type · the offer
Webinar FunnelThe offer arrives once, live, near the end. It has to survive being heard once with no scroll-back — so the guarantee does a lot of work.
Workshop · ChallengeTwo offers: the entry price that gets them in, and the ascension offer on the final day. The first one's real job is to qualify, not to profit.
Reverse SqueezeThe offer is never spoken until Part 2. Part 1's only job is to make the mechanism believable — so your mechanism has to be demonstrable, not just describable.
Other types: tripwire and free-plus-shipping funnels put the profit entirely in the upsell, so the front offer can lose money on purpose · a book funnel's offer is the call, not the book · a downsell funnel needs a second offer written before launch, not after the first one underperforms.

Step 3 — Pick Your Funnel Type

There's no "best" funnel — only the right one for your offer, your price, and how much your audience already believes. Twenty types, four families. Find the family first; the type inside it is a detail.

Twenty funnel types, grouped by the job they do
◆ the three shapes we build in depth — reverse squeeze has two variantshours = one-time build estimate, not ongoing load
Every one of the twenty still runs the same six stages from the master map. What the type decides is which stage carries the weight — and therefore where your build hours go.
◆ Example · same offer, three different types

A consultant selling a $999 programme could run any of three. Webinar if their audience is list-addressable and needs one idea reframed. Workshop if the product is the implementation and they can charge a small entry price to filter. Reverse squeeze if nobody's heard of them and the mechanism can be demonstrated in a single piece of content. Same offer. The choice is about belief and reach, not about the product.

Task 1.5Choose Your Type — and Write Down Why

Answer the three questions across the top of the diagram, in order. Then name your type and write one sentence saying which answer decided it. That sentence is what you'll check against on Friday when you're tempted to change everything.

Budget the hours honestly. The estimate next to your type is one-time build, before any traffic. Add the weekly running load: roughly 8–12 h/week for a webinar funnel, 10–15 during a live workshop cohort, 4–8 for a reverse squeeze.

OwnerYouToolNoneTime15 minDeliverableNamed funnel type + the deciding reasonProofBuild hours are in your calendar, not just your notes

Step 4 — Write Down the Arithmetic

Last thing today. Before you build anything, you write the equation that says whether this can work — and you write it in quantities you will actually be able to fetch, not in conversion rates you made up.

This is the single biggest difference between a funnel that gets optimised and one that gets abandoned. A rate you invented can never be wrong, so it never teaches you anything. A counted event can be wrong tomorrow, which is exactly what makes it useful.

Every term is a counted event with a named source
Today you'll fill this in with holes. That's correct. Anything you can't count yet gets written as unknown — will measure, and Day 3 is where you instrument it so it stops being unknown.
◆ Do this · the honest baseline

Write the equation out with your own numbers. For every term you have real data for, put the number and where it came from. For every term you don't, write "unknown — will measure" and move on. Do not fill a gap with a benchmark you read somewhere. A funnel modelled on borrowed averages will be optimised toward someone else's business.

Task 1.6Set Your Baseline and Your Target

Two lines of arithmetic, working backwards:

  1. The revenue you want, per month. A real number.
  2. Divide by your core offer price → buyers needed per month.
  3. Divide by whatever purchase rate you can actually evidence (or mark unknown) → qualified people needed.
  4. Keep going up the chain until you reach visits needed. That number is your traffic target — and it's the number Day 3's second half is built around.

If the visits number is absurd, you've learned something valuable on Day 1 rather than in month three: your price, your offer, or your funnel type has to change.

OwnerYouToolCalculator below, or a sheetTime30 minDeliverableBaseline equation + traffic targetProofEvery term is either sourced or explicitly marked unknown
◆ What changes per funnel type · the math
Webinar FunnelAn extra term almost everyone forgets: show-up rate. Registrations are not attendees, and the gap between them is the single most improvable number in the whole model.
Workshop · ChallengeTwo purchase events, not one — entry and ascension. Model them separately or the entry price will look like a failure when it's doing its actual job.
Reverse SqueezeThe leak moves upstream: your r1 isn't opt-in rate, it's consumption depth. Measure how far into Part 1 they get, because that's what predicts everything after it.
Other types: tripwire and free-plus-shipping funnels are modelled on contribution margin, not revenue — the front end is allowed to lose money · a book funnel's real conversion event is the booked call · JV funnels need the revenue-share percentage inside the equation from day one, not bolted on after.
◆ Your Day 1 output — half one

Your funnel strategy on one page: the ICP and the person inside it, the offer sentence, the ladder it sits on, the funnel type you're building and why, and the baseline arithmetic with its gaps marked. Plus your full 3-day work plan. Every other day is generated from this document — which is why it's worth being uncomfortable about how specific it is.

◆ Tonight's homework · 20 minutes

Send the five ICP questions to five real customers. Tomorrow you turn today's decisions into the conversion engine — the single source of context every page, email and ad gets generated from. Thin answers today make a thin engine tomorrow.

Half two · the conversion engine

Turn Those Decisions Into a Machine That Writes Everything

The first half gave you answers: who, what, which shape. On their own they are a document. This half turns them into one structured source of truth that every page, email, ad and outreach message gets generated from — so your funnel tells one story instead of nine.

Funnel vs. Campaign — Know the Difference

CampaignA MomentA launch, a promo, a burst. Has a start and an end. Great for spikes, useless for stability.
FunnelA MachineAlways on. A stranger can enter today, next week or next year and get the same journey. This is the asset.

Campaigns give you a good week. Funnels give you a predictable business. You'll run campaigns into your funnel — but the funnel is what you own.

◆ Why this distinction costs people money

Most businesses rebuild their messaging every campaign. New launch, new deck, new landing page, new emails — all written from scratch, all slightly different. Three campaigns later nobody can say what the company actually promises. A conversion engine makes that impossible, because every asset is derived from the same block of context rather than re-invented.

Step 1 — Write the Five Context Blocks

Here's the insight most people miss: your landing page, your emails, your ads, your outreach — they all draw from the same well. Define it once and every asset stays consistent. Change it once and everything downstream updates.

Define 5 inputs once → generate every asset
Context you define onceAssets it generates on demand
BlockWhat goes in itThe test that it's done
1 · OfferThe one-sentence offer from Day 1, the price at each rung, the guarantee, what's included, what's explicitly notA stranger can repeat your offer back correctly
2 · ICPAll ten ICP fields plus the persona card — and the verbatim objectionYou could hand it to a list-builder and get a usable list
3 · BrandVoice (three adjectives and three anti-adjectives), words you always use, words you never use, colours, type, logo rulesTwo different writers produce copy that sounds like one person
4 · MechanismYour named method, the 3–5 steps inside it, and why each step is necessaryIt explains why the obvious alternative fails
5 · ProofResults with numbers, named testimonials, logos, screenshots, third-party data — each tagged to the objection it answersEvery objection in block 2 has at least one proof against it
◆ Pro tip · name your mechanism

An unnamed method is a commodity. A named one is intellectual property. "We do outreach" is a service anyone sells; "The Compounding Invite System — four steps, and here's why step three is the one everyone skips" is a reason to choose you. Name it today. You'll use that name on every page you build tomorrow.

Task 2.1Fill All Five Blocks in One Document

One file, five headings, no design. Paste yesterday's Day-1 output straight into blocks 1 and 2 — that's what it was for. Then write blocks 3, 4 and 5 fresh.

Block 5 is where people cheat. Do not write "great results." Write a number, a name, and a date. If you have none, say so honestly and use borrowed proof — third-party research, a public case study, your own before-and-after — and label it as borrowed. An empty proof block is a survivable problem. A fake one is not.

OwnerYouToolAny doc, filled live during the sessionTime60 minDeliverableConversion engine documentProofEvery objection in block 2 has a matching proof in block 5

Step 2 — Build the Diagnose-Then-Prescribe Engine

Here's the deal: the highest-converting thing you can do to a stranger is not pitch them. It's diagnose them — and then prescribe. People don't argue with a conclusion they helped produce.

This mechanic works everywhere. It's a poll inside a live session, a qualification form on a registration page, an opt-in question on a reverse squeeze bridge, or a full scored assessment. Same engine, different wrapper.

Ask → score → band → prescribe (the reusable engine)
The band is the story, the score is the hook. A number gets attention. The band — "you're conversion-limited" — is what makes the recommendation feel inevitable rather than sold.
◆ Example · the same engine in four wrappers

In a live session: four polls, and the poll answers segment your follow-up. On a registration page: two qualification fields that route registrants into different reminder sequences. On a reverse squeeze bridge: one question between Part 1 and Part 2 that decides which Part 2 they get. As a standalone assessment: the full scored quiz with a gauge and a paywall. Same ask → score → band → prescribe. The only thing that changes is how many questions you can get away with.

Task 2.2Design Your Diagnostic
  1. Name 3–5 score axes. These are the dimensions your offer actually improves. If your offer fixes conversion, one axis is conversion. Don't invent axes you can't help with.
  2. Write 6–12 agreement statements and tag each to an axis. Statements, not questions: "I know which step of my funnel leaks the most" — agree/disagree.
  3. Write the three band labels — one per likely weak axis. These become headlines later.
  4. Write the band → rung rule and commit to it in writing.

Keep it short. Every extra question costs you completions, and a 12-statement diagnostic that people finish beats a 30-statement one they abandon.

OwnerYouToolDoc, then the spec tomorrowTime45 minDeliverableAxes · statements · bands · the mapping ruleProofEvery statement maps to exactly one axis you can improve
◆ What changes per funnel type · the diagnostic
Webinar FunnelIt becomes polls — three of them, run live. Poll answers are the highest-intent segmentation signal you'll get all week, so tag them into the CRM the moment they're cast.
Workshop · ChallengeIt becomes the daily survey. You get three chances to ask instead of one — so spread it, and let each day's answers personalise the next day's output.
Reverse SqueezeIt becomes the opt-in bridge. One or two questions maximum, placed between Part 1 and Part 2, where the value has already been delivered and they owe you an answer.
Other types: a book-a-call funnel puts the diagnostic on the booking form, where it doubles as call prep · tripwire and free-plus-shipping funnels diagnose after purchase, to pick which upsell to show · a community funnel diagnoses on join, to route people to the right channel.

Step 3 — Put It All in One File

Now the part that turns a document into an engine. Everything you just wrote — brand, ICP, offer, pricing, the statements, the bands, the rule — goes into one structured file. Not five documents. One.

Why it matters: a page built from a file can be changed by editing the file. A page built by hand can only be changed by whoever built it, in the place they built it, if they remember where. One file is the difference between a funnel you can tune and a funnel you have to rebuild.

One spec file → one renderer → every asset, and every experiment
You don't have to write the file by hand. Tomorrow you describe it and your AI writes it. But you have to know what belongs in it — which is exactly what today produced.
◆ The rule that makes this work

Nothing per-brand gets hardcoded. If a headline, a price, a question or an event name lives inside the page code rather than the spec, you've just created work for your future self — and guaranteed that changing it needs a developer. Copy, prices, questions, score rules, event names and experiment variants all live in the file. The code only knows how to render.

Task 2.3Write the Spec Outline — Keys Only

You're not writing JSON today. You're writing the outline: the list of keys and what each one holds. Nine top-level sections is plenty:

  • brand · icp · offer · pricing — straight from your five blocks
  • stages — the six from the master map, each with its screens
  • scoreModel — the axes, statements and the band rule from Task 2.2
  • copy — headlines and CTAs, one per screen
  • analytics — the event names from your Day-1 arithmetic
  • experiments — empty today, filled from Day 3 onward

Tomorrow's build reads this outline. An hour here saves a day there.

OwnerYou · your AI drafts itToolClaude Code, or any AITime30 minDeliverableSpec outline, nine sectionsProofNothing in it is a design decision — it's all content and rules
◆ What changes per funnel type · the spec
Webinar FunnelAdd an event section: date, time, duration, timezone handling, and the replay window. Everything in S3 reads its timings from that one place — change the date once, every reminder moves.
Workshop · ChallengeAdd a days[] array — three entries, each with its session, its survey questions, and the output it generates. The daily loop is data, not three hand-built pages.
Reverse SqueezeAdd contentParts[] with watch-depth thresholds. Your whole branching logic keys off "how far did they get", so those thresholds belong in the spec where you can tune them.
Other types: product-launch funnels add a dated open/close cart window · free-plus-shipping adds shipping zones and COGS so margin is computable · JV funnels add a partners[] block with revenue-share percentages, because attribution has to be unambiguous before money moves.
◆ Your Day 1 output — half two

A conversion engine: five context blocks filled, a diagnostic designed (axes, statements, bands, mapping rule), and a spec outline that tomorrow's build reads directly. This is the single source of truth every asset on Day 2 gets generated from.

Day 2Funnel Elements · Every Page, Template and Stage

Build Every Element — The Whole Funnel, Assembled

Today the engine becomes assets. You work stage by stage, S1 to S6, and at the end of it every page, every message and every automation trigger exists as something you could hand to someone else.

◆ Build in this order, and only this order

The funnel core before the traffic. Build S2 through S5 first — the pages, the sequences, the close — then attach S1 on top. People do it backwards, switch on traffic into a half-built funnel, and burn a list they can never un-burn. Traffic is the cheapest thing to add and the most expensive thing to waste.

The Path a Visitor Actually Moves Through

The path a visitor actually moves through — with the branch that matters
The branch is the point. A drip sends everyone the same five emails. A funnel checks "are they ready?" and routes accordingly — buyers to checkout, everyone else into a loop that re-offers when the timing's right.

Traffic

S1 — The Traffic Engine

Five channels. Each one has hard operating limits, and each limit exists because someone learned it the expensive way — a burned domain, a restricted account, a list that can never be emailed again.

Daily operating limits, and the weekly scale-or-fix gate
The diagnosis is in which number is low. A weak open rate is a deliverability problem — a domain and warm-up issue. A weak click-through is an offer problem, and no amount of inbox tuning will fix it.
Task 3.1Stand Up the Sending Infrastructure Before You Write a Word
  1. Buy separate domains for outreach. Never your main brand domain — if it gets flagged, your invoices stop arriving too.
  2. Point DNS at your provider and set SPF, DKIM and DMARC. All three. Missing any one of them halves your inbox placement.
  3. Create your sending accounts and put them straight into warm-up for 2–3 weeks. Yes, that's before the workshop ends. Start today and they're ready when your funnel is.
  4. Validate your list. Target under 1% bounce, and reject any purchased file with more than 1–2% duplicates.
OwnerYouToolDomain registrar · DNS · sending platformTime90 min setup, then 2–3 weeks of waitingDeliverableAuthenticated domains in warm-upProofA test send lands in the primary inbox, not promotions
Task 3.2Write Two Variants per Channel, Not One

One variant gives you a result. Two give you a comparison — and a comparison is the only thing that teaches you anything. Generate both from your conversion engine so they share the offer and differ only in angle:

  • Variant A · benefit-led — lead with the dream outcome from your value equation.
  • Variant B · problem-led — lead with the verbatim objection from your ICP card.

Same for ads, same for LinkedIn messages, same for content hooks. And run every link through your UTM scheme — a channel you can't attribute is a channel you can't defend at budget time.

OwnerYou · AI drafts from the engineToolClaude Code, or any AITime60 minDeliverable2 variants × every live channel, UTM-taggedProofBoth variants trace back to a block in your engine
◆ What changes per funnel type · traffic
Webinar FunnelTraffic is dated — every asset carries a date and expires. Run the invite push in a concentrated window, and change the event date a few minutes before you go live so the listing re-ranks for the next cycle.
Workshop · ChallengeTraffic is cohort-shaped, and peer referral is a real channel: participants recruit participants. Give them a shareable link with their own tag on it from day one.
Reverse SqueezeTraffic points at content, not a form — so it never expires and it accumulates. The same link works for the next twelve months, which changes what a click is worth.
Other types: product launches concentrate everything into a dated open-cart window · hub-and-spoke and community funnels run permanently-on evergreen traffic · JV funnels replace your traffic entirely with a partner's list, which means your real S1 work is partner recruitment, not ad creative.

Stage 1 at a Glance: The Traffic Engine

Six channels, one lead list, one tracking scheme and one weekly gate. Set these up before any channel.

1The Full Setup
2The Task

Stage 1 sends the right people to your registration page. Before you touch any channel, set up the four things every channel shares: an approved buyer profile, one clean lead list, one link-tagging scheme and sending domains that are already warming up. Then switch on the channels that fit your offer and read their numbers once a week. You're done when every channel's links are tagged, every list is verified and a test contact from each channel lands in your CRM with its source attached.

How This Changes by Mechanism

Traffic is dated. Every asset carries the event date and expires with it, so run the invite push in a concentrated window before the session.

3Step by Step
  1. 1
    Pick the Channels You'll Run

    You don't need all six. Pick by how warm your audience already is:

    • Cold calendar and cold email reach people who have never heard of you. They need domains and 2–3 weeks of warm-up.
    • LinkedIn outreach reaches named people through your own profile.
    • Blog and social compound over time and cost nothing per click.
    • Paid ads are the fastest to switch on and the fastest to burn budget.

    Each channel has hard daily limits. They exist because someone lost a domain or an account learning them.

  2. 2
    Get Your Buyer Profile Approved in Writing

    Every outreach channel pulls from the same description of who you're for. Write it down: job titles, company size, the region they buy in, and whether your contact is the buyer or the signer.

    Get it approved in writing before you pay anyone for a list. A list bought against the wrong profile is money you don't get back, and every re-scoped list is a new invoice.

    Tip Check that the job titles you picked actually exist as filters in the data tool you'll use.

    Capture Needed

    An approved buyer persona card from the template library (buyer-persona-card) rendered full width.

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  3. 3
    Tag Every Link Before You Share It

    A UTM is a short tag on the end of a link that tells your analytics which channel sent the visitor. Without it, you can't tell which channel earned a registration, and you can't defend the budget.

    1. Open Google's free Campaign URL Builder ↗.
    2. Paste your registration page link.
    3. Fill in source (calendar, email, linkedin, meta, google, blog, social), medium and campaign.
    4. Copy the finished link. Never type a tagged link by hand.
  4. 4
    Start Warming Domains Today

    Cold calendar and cold email send from separate domains, never your main one. If an outreach domain gets flagged, your invoices and client email keep working.

    New inboxes need 2–3 weeks of warm-up before they can send to real prospects. Buy the domains and start the warm-up now, so they're ready when your funnel is. The Cold Email guide below walks through every click.

  5. 5
    Build One Clean Lead List

    Buy or build one list, then clean it once for every channel:

    1. Remove duplicates, including people on lists you already have.
    2. Delete rows with no email or no first name.
    3. Verify every email. Keep only addresses the checker confirms. Aim for under 1% bounce.
    4. Remove everyone on your do-not-contact list, everyone already contacted and everyone who already registered.

    Reject any bought file with more than 1–2% duplicates.

  6. 6
    Work Out How Much You Can Send

    Count the working days until your event. Multiply by what your accounts can safely send each day. That's how many people you can actually reach.

    If your list is bigger than that, the answer is more inboxes or an earlier start. Never raise the daily limit on an account to catch up.

    Tip Scale in steps. A sudden jump in volume is the clearest signal a spam filter reads.

  7. 7
    Write Two Versions for Every Channel

    One version gives you a result. Two give you a comparison, which is the only thing that teaches you anything.

    • Version A, benefit-led: open with the outcome your buyer wants.
    • Version B, problem-led: open with the objection, in your buyer's own words.

    Generate both from your conversion engine, so they share the offer and differ only in angle.

  8. 8
    Record Every Send in One Sheet

    Keep one master outreach sheet with a tab per event. Column A is the date each person was contacted. Fill it in only after the send is confirmed, never before.

    That single column is what stops anyone being contacted twice across calendar, email and LinkedIn.

    Tip Work by column name, not column letter. Columns move every time someone pastes data in.

    Capture Needed

    A Google Sheet laid out as the master outreach sheet (column A 'Send date', then email, first name, company, channel status columns) with anonymised rows.

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  9. 9
    Read the Numbers Once a Week

    Every week, for each channel, pick one of three moves:

    • Scale it: click-through at least 3%, conversion at least 1.5% and bounce at most 2%. Add inboxes or budget, not new ideas.
    • Fix it today: open rate under 15%, click-through under 1% or bounce over 5%. Stop sending from that inbox now.
    • Hold and tune: anything in between. Change exactly one thing, then measure again.

    A low open rate is a deliverability problem. A low click-through is an offer problem.

The Firefighting Ops Head

Head of Operations · 200–1,000-person mid-market distribution business · 3–8 depots · owns planning, dispatch and the carrier budget

The Job

Measured on

On-time delivery and cost per stop, reviewed weekly with the depot managers.

Reports upward

Cost per stop and service level to the COO or CFO every month; a cost-increase explanation every quarter.

Top Pains, in Their Words

  • "This morning's plan broke before the vans left."
  • "I can't tell finance why cost per stop went up."
  • "My best planners spend the day firefighting."

Top Outcomes, in Their Words

  • "A plan that holds before 7am."
  • "A cost number I can defend in the review."
  • "Planners who plan instead of patching."

Buying Triggers

  • A new depot or a big new customer
  • A carrier rate increase or surcharge announcement
  • A quarterly review with no answer to 'why did cost go up?'
  • A senior planner resigning

Objections and Reframes

Good. We don't start by replacing it; we start by showing which runs it plans on capacity they never needed.

Watering Holes

  • Logistics trade press and newsletters
  • Operations and supply-chain LinkedIn groups
  • Regional distribution events and carrier user groups
  • Peers at other depots, by phone

Disqualifiers: Looks Like Them, Isn't

  • Single-van operators with fixed daily routes
  • Pure parcel shippers who outsource all delivery
  • Teams mid-way through a system replacement with no budget until it lands

Cold Calendar

Put the session straight into a prospect's calendar from warmed inboxes, with Tantra and Google.

1The Full Setup
2The Task

Send calendar invites for your session from your warmed outreach inboxes, so it appears in the prospect's own calendar. You'll give Tantra permission to create events through a Google service account, add your sending inboxes with safe daily caps, import a verified list and run the campaign wizard. You're done when a test invite shows up in a real calendar, the campaign's events × guests matches your list, and every reply updates your CRM without anyone touching it.

How This Changes by Mechanism

The invite is the session itself: title, date and join details. Send the whole list 5–9 days before.

3Step by Step
  1. 1
    Create a Google Cloud Project

    Sign in to console.cloud.google.com ↗ with your Google Workspace account. A personal @gmail.com account can't do this.

    1. Open the project dropdown at the top and click New Project.
    2. Name it for the job and pick your organisation. Click Create.
    3. Open APIs & Services → Library. Search Gmail API and click Enable. Do the same for Google Calendar API.

    Both should now appear under *Enabled APIs & Services*.

  2. 2
    Create the Service Account and Its Key

    A service account is a robot login that lets Tantra create calendar events for your inboxes.

    1. Open IAM & Admin → Service Accounts → Create service account. Name it (for example, Calendar Automation) and click Create and Continue.
    2. Give it the Basic → Owner role, then Done.
    3. On the account, open ⋮ → Manage keys → Add key → Create new key → JSON. The file downloads.

    Treat that file as a password. Never email it, upload it anywhere else or put it in a repo. If it leaks, delete the key on the same screen and make a new one that day.

  3. 3
    Unblock Key Creation When It's Greyed Out

    Some organisations block service account keys by default. If Create new key is greyed out:

    1. Switch to organisation view (click the project picker and select the organisation).
    2. In IAM & Admin → IAM, edit your own user and add the role Organisation Policy Administrator.
    3. In IAM & Admin → Organisation Policies, open each of these three: *Block service account bindings*, *Disable service account creation*, *Disable service account key creation*.
    4. For each: Manage Policy → Override parent's policy → Add a Rule → Enforcement: Off → Done → Set Policy.

    Tip This changes a security setting for the whole organisation. Only do it on the organisation you set up for outreach.

    Capture Needed

    Google Cloud Console → IAM & Admin → Organisation Policies → one of the three policies with 'Override parent's policy' and 'Enforcement: Off' selected.

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  4. 4
    Allow the Service Account to Act for Your Inboxes
    1. In Service Accounts, open the account and copy its Client ID (under Details → Advanced settings).
    2. Sign in to admin.google.com ↗ as a Super Admin.
    3. Open Security → Access and data control → API controls → Domain-wide delegation → Add new.
    4. Paste the Client ID and these five scopes on one line, separated by commas:

    https://www.googleapis.com/auth/calendar, https://www.googleapis.com/auth/calendar.events, https://www.googleapis.com/auth/gmail.send, https://www.googleapis.com/auth/userinfo.email, https://www.googleapis.com/auth/userinfo.profile

    1. Click Authorize. It can take minutes, and occasionally up to an hour, to work. Wait before redoing it.
  5. 5
    Connect Tantra and Add Your Senders
    1. Log in to Tantra with Continue with Google. Your first login creates the workspace.
    2. Open Connectors → Google Service Accounts and upload the JSON key. Nothing can send until this is done.
    3. Open Accounts and paste your sending inbox addresses, one per line.
    4. Select them all and set each inbox's daily limit. The agreed cap is 200 calendar requests a day per account, and the default has been higher, so set it on purpose rather than inheriting it.
    5. Set each inbox's warm status (cold or warm) and save.

    A cold inbox is capped far lower. Tantra spreads a big list over later days rather than go over the cap.

  6. 6
    Use the Same Warmed Domains as Cold Email

    Calendar invites go out from real inboxes, so they need the same DNS records and warm-up as cold email: SPF, DKIM, DMARC and MX, checked in three free tools. Follow steps 3–6 of the Cold Email guide if you haven't already.

    On a cold inbox, start at 20 invites a day and move to 50 once it's warmed. Never send from your main brand domain.

  7. 7
    Import Your Contacts

    Importing is safe. Nothing sends yet.

    1. Open Contacts → Import Contacts and drop in your verified CSV. The import screen shows the most one upload can hold; split anything bigger.
    2. Map the columns and check the email column is mapped to Email.
    3. Click Add to a list → Create new list, name it {event_title} - {date}, then select it.
    4. Click Import Contacts and wait for the done message.
  8. 8
    Write the Invite Description

    The description is the only copy the prospect reads. Keep it short:

    • The first lines are the promise. Put the join link lower down.
    • Add one line that makes declining easy, so fewer people report it.
    • No em dashes, no $, % or 'free' in the title.
    • Every link carries utm_source=calendar.

    Keep a copy of the approved text. You'll check the live campaign against it.

  9. 9
    Run the Wizard Carefully: Finishing It Sends

    Tantra has no draft. The moment you finish the wizard, invites go out, unless you set a future date.

    1. Campaigns → Create Campaign, name it and click Next.
    2. Select the list you just imported.
    3. Pick your senders on purpose. Rotate sets between days and check none is already busy today.
    4. Set the event title, start and end time, and paste the approved description.
    5. On the review screen, check the contact count, event time and sender count, and read the description in full.
    6. Only then click Launch Smart Campaign → Yes, Launch.

    Tip Run the outreach pre-launch gate first. If any box is unticked, don't launch.

  10. 10
    Check It Sent, Then Wait

    Open Campaigns → your campaign → ⋮ → View.

    • The campaign isn't paused.
    • The number of events × guests matches your list size.
    • The Contacts tab shows each person's RSVP.

    Sending can take up to 13 minutes to start, and the counters read zero the whole time. Don't create a second campaign because it looks stuck. That's how people get invited twice.

  11. 11
    Let Every Reply Update Your CRM

    An automation reads the sending inboxes every 60 seconds:

    • Accepted or tentative: the person is registered for the session and their contact gets the RSVP.
    • Declined: the contact is updated, with no registration.
    • A bounce notice: the contact is flagged as bounced and goes on your do-not-contact list.

    Claude Code builds this for you as a small script. There's no extra tool to buy. See the prompt below.

  12. 12
    Record the Send and Report Honestly
    1. Export the sent list from Contacts → Export CSV.
    2. Match it against your master outreach sheet and write the send date in column A for exactly those rows. Only after sending is confirmed.

    Two reporting rules:

    • An RSVP isn't a registration. Report the people registered in your event platform.
    • A tool's counter isn't proof of delivery. Check the sending inbox's own calendar.
    Capture Needed

    Tantra → Dashboard → Calendar Campaigns showing invitations sent and meetings booked (anonymised).

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

Build the RSVP and Bounce Reader
Build me a small automation that checks my outreach inboxes every 60 seconds. For each new message: if the subject says the delivery failed, find the recipient in my CRM and mark them bounced (create them if they're missing) and add them to my do-not-contact list. Otherwise read the calendar reply: 'accepted' = yes, 'tentatively accepted' = maybe, 'declined' = no. Update the contact's rsvp_status with source 'Google Calendar Outreach'. For yes or maybe, register them for the session in my event platform. Skip anything already processed. Show me a test run on three sample messages before it goes live.

S1 · Traffic

Cold Email

Domains, inboxes, DNS, warm-up, a verified list and a five-step thread that stops on reply.

1The Full Setup
2The Task

Build a cold email channel that reaches inboxes, not spam folders. You'll buy separate outreach domains, create inboxes on them, prove they're authenticated, warm them up for 2–3 weeks, and send a five-step thread from Instantly to a verified list. You're done when every domain passes all three checkers, every inbox shows warm-up on, and a test email lands in a real primary inbox.

Steps
13
Examples
8
Runs On
Namecheap · Google Workspace · Apollo · Cloudflare · Instantly · Google Sheets · Calendly

How This Changes by Mechanism

Every email carries the session date. Finish the thread before the event; step 4 is the date and the booking link.

3Step by Step
  1. 1
    Buy Separate Outreach Domains

    Never send cold email from your main domain. If it gets flagged, your normal email stops arriving too.

    1. Write 2 branded names and 5 anonymised ones (topic + format, like {topic}sessions.com).
    2. On Namecheap, open Domains → Domain Name Search and switch to Beast Mode, its bulk search.
    3. Paste all seven at once.
    4. Untick Show Premiums and tick Hide Unavailable, then search.
    5. Add your shortlist to the cart. Confirm it with the owner before you pay.
  2. 2
    Create the Inboxes

    Each domain gets a few mailboxes on Google Workspace. You choose the usernames (first names read best).

    If an inbox provider sets them up for you, give them everything in one go: the domains, the usernames per domain, registrar access and your Instantly login. Create the Instantly account first, because their form asks for it.

    Tip When they finish, change every password you shared with them. Instantly: Settings → Account → change password.

  3. 3
    Add the Four DNS Records

    DNS records prove to inbox providers that your mail is really from you. In Cloudflare, open the domain, then DNS → Records → Add record.

    • MX (5 records): ASPMX.L.GOOGLE.COM priority 1, ALT1 and ALT2 priority 5, ALT3 and ALT4 priority 10.
    • SPF (TXT, name @): v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com ~all
    • DKIM (TXT, name google._domainkey): the key from the next step.
    • DMARC (TXT, name _dmarc): v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:{you}; ruf=mailto:{you}; fo=1

    Delete any old MX records first. Keep exactly one SPF record: two break authentication without any error message.

  4. 4
    Generate the DKIM Key in Google
    1. In the Google Admin console, open Apps → Google Workspace → Gmail → Authenticate email.
    2. Pick the domain and click Generate new record (keep the selector as google).
    3. Copy the value into the DKIM record in Cloudflare.
    4. Come back and click Start authentication.

    Repeat for every domain.

  5. 5
    Check Every Domain in Three Free Tools

    Check every domain before anything sends:

    1. Google Admin Toolbox ↗ checks MX, SPF and DKIM in one go.
    2. MXToolbox ↗ → Domain Health gives a full report.
    3. DNS Checker ↗ shows whether the records have spread worldwide.

    A pass looks like this: SPF present, DKIM valid, DMARC found, MX pointing at Google, and nothing listed twice. If DKIM fails, generate a new key, replace the record and click Start authentication again.

  6. 6
    Connect the Inboxes and Start Warm-Up

    Warm-up sends and replies to a small number of friendly emails each day so inbox providers learn to trust a new account.

    1. In Instantly, open Email Accounts. Every inbox should say *Connected*.
    2. Switch Warmup on for every inbox. Leave it on even after campaigns go live.
    3. Set each inbox's Daily limit to 20. Raise it to 50 once warm-up looks clean.

    New inboxes need 2–3 weeks before they join a live campaign.

  7. 7
    Add a Tracking Domain

    A tracking domain makes open and click numbers trustworthy and keeps links from sharing a tool-wide reputation.

    1. In Instantly, open Settings → Tracking domain and add a subdomain.
    2. Copy the CNAME record Instantly shows you into Cloudflare.
    3. Come back and confirm it reads active.

    Don't quote any click number until this is active.

  8. 8
    Clean and Verify the List

    Work on a copy of the file you bought. Keep the original as your receipt.

    1. Check the row count matches the invoice.
    2. Add a helper column with =LOWER(TRIM(C2)) and remove duplicates with Data → Data cleanup → Remove duplicates.
    3. Delete rows with no email or no first name.
    4. Verify every address. Keep only confirmed ones. Unknown or accept-all is not a yes.
    5. Remove do-not-contact, already contacted, past registrants, bounces and unsubscribes.
  9. 9
    Build the Campaign and Import the Leads
    1. In Instantly, open Campaigns → Create new campaign and name it after the event and channel.
    2. Open Leads → Import → Upload CSV.
    3. Map every column carefully: email, first name, company.

    A wrong mapping personalises every email wrongly, and you won't see it until it sends.

  10. 10
    Write the Five-Step Thread

    Open the Sequences tab and write five steps with these waits: +0, +3, +3, +3, +4 days.

    • Only step 1 has a subject line. Steps 2–5 have none, so they arrive as replies in the same thread.
    • Put an unsubscribe line in every step.
    • Use only tokens Instantly understands: {{firstName}} and {{companyName}}.
    • If a name is missing, drop it from the sentence instead of printing a placeholder.
    • No em dashes. Every link carries utm_source=email.
  11. 11
    Set the Schedule and the Campaign Limit
    1. Under Accounts inside the campaign, pick the inboxes that will send it.
    2. Under Schedule, send Monday to Friday, in business hours in your audience's time zone.
    3. Under Options, set the campaign's daily limit and check Stop on reply is on.

    The campaign's own limit is the one that counts. Set it to 200 across inboxes that allow 400 and you waste half your capacity with no warning.

  12. 12
    Send a Test, Pass the Gate, Then Launch

    Send yourself a test. Check the tokens filled in and it landed in the primary inbox, not spam.

    Then run the pre-launch gate: warmed inboxes, a verified list with no overlap, copy read inside the tool, unsubscribe on every step, tagged links, and a booking link you've opened in a real browser that shows open slots.

    Instantly creates campaigns stopped. Nothing goes out until you press Launch.

  13. 13
    Handle Replies and Bounces Every Day

    Each day, check sent, opens, replies and bounces in Analytics, and any inbox showing an error or paused warm-up in Email Accounts.

    • An interested reply: answer it from the Unibox and send the registration or booking link. Stop on reply ends their sequence.
    • A bounce or unsubscribe: add them to your do-not-contact list and block them in every tool, not just Instantly.
    • Deliverability slipping: pause. Don't push through.

    Then stamp the send date in column A of your master sheet.

Outreach Pre-launch Gate

SaaSConsultingServicesAI

S1 · Traffic

LinkedIn Outreach

Connect, follow up and invite through HeyReach inside safe daily limits, plus a company event page.

1The Full Setup
2The Task

Reach named people through your own LinkedIn profile without risking the account. You'll connect your profile to HeyReach, set daily limits, import one clean list, and build a sequence that only messages people who accepted. You'll also publish an event on your company page that links to your registration page. You're done when the campaign is running under the limits, every link carries utm_source=linkedin and event sign-ups flow into your CRM.

Steps
10
Examples
7
Runs On
HeyReach · LinkedIn · Google Sheets · GoHighLevel

How This Changes by Mechanism

The event page date must match the event platform to the minute. Every message before the date points at registration.

3Step by Step
  1. 1
    Connect Your LinkedIn Account to HeyReach

    You connect your own account. Nobody else should ever hold your LinkedIn password.

    1. Log in to HeyReach and open LinkedIn Accounts in the left sidebar.
    2. Click Add account and follow the connection method it offers.
    3. Complete any LinkedIn security check on your own device.
    4. Check the account now shows as connected.

    A 'not active' label usually just means no campaign is running yet. It doesn't mean the account can't send.

  2. 2
    Set Your Daily Limits

    Open the account's daily activity settings and set:

    • Connection requests: 20–25 a day to start. Ramp up slowly as the account ages, never past 75.
    • Messages: 50 a day.
    • InMail: 30 a day.

    All messaging across every campaign on one account stays under 75 a day in total. Going over risks the account, and there is no appeal.

  3. 3
    Import One Clean List
    1. Open Lists → Create new list (or Leads → Add Leads).
    2. Upload your CSV of profile links, map the columns and import.

    Get the list right before you import it. There's no button to remove a lead afterwards, and re-importing a cleaned version doesn't fix it. A campaign's list can't be changed once the campaign exists, so always build the list first.

  4. 4
    Create One Campaign per Voice
    1. Open Campaigns → Start a new Campaign.
    2. Put the sender's name in the campaign name. You'll end up with one campaign per voice.
    3. Select your list.

    HeyReach can't change the wording per sender inside one campaign. If the founder and a team member both send, that's two campaigns and two lists with no one on both.

  5. 5
    Build the Sequence With an Accepted Branch

    In the step builder, start with a connection request, then add the accepted / not accepted branch. Only people who accept get messages.

    Send follow-ups 0, 3, 7, 12 and 25 days after they accept:

    • Use only {FIRST_NAME} and {COMPANY}. Other formats look fine in the builder and print nothing.
    • If a name is missing, drop it from the sentence.
    • Every link carries utm_source=linkedin.
  6. 6
    Set the Not-Accepted Wait in Days

    The wait on the not-accepted side is how long someone has to accept. Set it in days, not hours. If it's set to hours, a person who accepts on day two never gets a message.

    Also check auto-withdraw. If invites withdraw at day 14, the real window ends at day 14, whatever the branch says.

  7. 7
    Pick the Senders and Re-Check Them

    Choose the sending account and set its limits for this campaign. Right before you start, open the sender list again. Sender assignments have been seen to change on their own, so look instead of assuming.

  8. 8
    Start the Campaign

    HeyReach creates campaigns as drafts. Nothing sends until you press Launch campaign.

    Before you do, read every message once more in the builder against your approved copy and open every link in a real browser.

  9. 9
    Publish an Event on Your Company Page

    An event gives LinkedIn a second, free path to your registration page.

    1. On your company page, open Admin tools → Create event.
    2. Match the name, date, time and time zone to your event platform exactly.
    3. Upload the banner.
    4. Set the external registration link to your registration page with ?utm_source=linkedin on the end.
    5. Publish, then use Invite to invite connections (140–150 a day).
    Capture Needed

    LinkedIn company page → Admin tools → Create event form (owner-session capture; LinkedIn is never opened by browser tools).

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  10. 10
    Export Event Sign-Ups and Check Daily

    The event's own sign-up list is a real lead source. Export it and run it through the same cleaning and exclusions as any other list, then register them and add them to your CRM.

    Every day, check the campaign's requests sent, accepted and failed. Rotate senders between days and scale in steps. Anyone who asks to stop goes on your do-not-contact list and HeyReach's exclude list.

Blog

One pillar post a month, drafted from your engine, tagged, published and read by clicks to page.

1The Full Setup
2The Task

Publish one pillar blog post that answers a question your buyer is already asking, and send its readers to your registration page. You'll pick the topic from your conversion engine, have AI draft it from that engine, set the search settings, tag every link, publish, then check the live page. You're done when the post is live, its call to action carries utm_source=blog, and a test click shows up in your analytics as blog traffic.

Steps
8
Examples
6
Runs On
Claude Code · Notion · GA4 · WordPress · Metricool · Beehiiv

How This Changes by Mechanism

The post is dated content. Its call to action carries the session date, so refresh the date and link before each new cycle.

3Step by Step
  1. 1
    Pick One Topic From Your Engine

    Take the topic from your conversion engine, not from a blank page. Choose one named pain point from your buyer profile, or this month's theme from your 12-topic rotation.

    Add it as a new page in your content calendar in Notion, with a title that makes a promise and has a number in it.

    Tip A thin answer in your engine makes a thin post. If the pain point isn't in your buyer profile, fix the profile first.

  2. 2
    Have AI Draft It From the Engine

    Give Claude Code (or any AI) your engine file and the post outline, not a one-line prompt. Use the prompt below.

    Then check the draft: every claim should trace back to something in your engine. Remove anything it made up, especially numbers.

    Capture Needed

    Claude Code terminal running the blog-draft prompt against an engine file, with the draft output visible.

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  3. 3
    Lay the Post Out in Your Blog Editor

    In WordPress, open Posts → Add New Post and paste the draft.

    • One H1 that states the promise.
    • A subheading for each idea.
    • One worked example.
    • One call to action to your session, near the end.

    Add a featured image. Keep paragraphs short. Most readers are on a phone.

  4. 4
    Fill Out the Search Settings

    Search settings decide how the post appears in Google.

    • Focus keyphrase: the words your buyer types.
    • Slug: the short web address, in plain words.
    • Meta description: one sentence that makes the promise.

    A plugin such as Yoast shows a traffic-light check as you type.

    Capture Needed

    The Yoast SEO panel in the WordPress editor with focus keyphrase, slug and meta description fields.

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  5. 5
    Tag the Call-to-Action Link

    Build the link in Google's Campaign URL Builder ↗:

    • Source: blog
    • Medium: organic
    • Campaign: {event_slug}_{date}

    Paste the finished link into the call to action. A channel you can't trace is a channel you can't defend at budget time.

  6. 6
    Publish, Then Read It Like a Stranger

    Click Publish. The post is public, and search engines can pick it up almost immediately.

    Open the live page on your phone and check:

    • The date is right, if the post mentions one.
    • The call-to-action link opens your registration page with the tag intact.
    • No stray dashes or leftover placeholders.
    Capture Needed

    A live published pillar post on a phone-width screen with the call-to-action block visible.

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  7. 7
    Hand It to the Social Guide

    This post is your pillar. Don't write social posts from scratch. Cut this one into five clips and a set of quotes (the Social guide shows how), and post about the event every 3 days.

    If you send a newsletter, the post also becomes that month's issue.

    Capture Needed

    Metricool planner with a batch of posts scheduled from one pillar (Metricool help centre).

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  8. 8
    Read Clicks to Page Every Week

    In Google Analytics, open Reports → Acquisition → Traffic acquisition and filter to source blog.

    Read clicks to your registration page first. Engagement isn't traffic. If clicks run at 3% or more of readers, keep going. Under 1%, the post isn't selling the session: change the call to action before anything else.

Draft the Pillar Post
Using my conversion engine file (offer, ICP, objections, method), draft a pillar blog post that answers this question my buyer is asking: [question]. Structure: a promise headline with a number, the problem in the buyer's words, three to five sections with subheadings (one idea each), one worked example from the engine, then an invite to my session on [date] with this link: [tagged link]. Use only facts and numbers that appear in the engine; if you need one that isn't there, write [NEEDS SOURCE]. Short paragraphs, plain words, no em dashes.

Express Capacity Is Powerful. Are You Using It on the Wrong Runs?

The premium service works. The problem is where it quietly spreads.

Maya Okonkwo · 6 min read

Premium delivery capacity is genuinely impressive. Dedicated vehicles, express carriers and guaranteed same-day slots deliver real value for the work they were designed for: tight customer windows, high-value or fragile loads, emergency replenishment, the delivery that simply can't be late.

But here's what happens in practice.

How the Default Spreads

A planner tries express capacity on one demanding customer. The results are excellent. Word spreads.

Within weeks, runs across the network are booked on premium capacity, whether or not the delivery justifies it. Routine weekly drops. Short shuttles between depots. Overnight replenishment that has run the same way for years.

All of them running at premium rates, for deliveries that would arrive in the same window, far more cheaply, on standard capacity.

Express is built for speed and certainty under pressure. Most deliveries aren't under that pressure.

The Cost Is Not Small

Premium rates are meaningfully higher than standard ones. Multiply that across hundreds of runs that never needed it, and the compounding cost becomes significant, and entirely invisible until contract renewal.

The Questions Your Team Should Ask Before Every Booking

  • Does this delivery have a window tight enough that standard capacity would genuinely miss it?
  • Does a customer promise require the certainty premium capacity provides?
  • Would standard capacity deliver the same outcome at a lower cost per stop?

What We Built to Answer Them

That's why Northwind maps every run booked on premium capacity across your depots, then classifies each one by window, load value and volume, and identifies which runs are paying premium prices for work that doesn't need them.

The output is a prioritised plan to move each run to right-sized capacity, with no manual analysis from your team.
