Pipeline Changes for a Webinar

Four event stages in front of Form Filled, and a checkout shortcut for lower-priced offers.

1The Full Setup
2The Task

Add the event stages in front of Form Filled so you can see who registered, who joined live, who missed it and who caught the replay. Give lower-priced offers a checkout that skips the call. Everything from Eval Call Scheduled onwards stays exactly as the shared pipeline. You're done when a test registrant who misses the live session lands in No-Show, and a test buyer reaches Payment Completed without passing through stages 2–8.

Steps
3
Examples
3
Runs On
WebinarGeek · Cal.com · Dodo Payments
3Step by Step
  1. 1
    Add Registered, Attended, No-Show and Replay Watched

    Add four columns to the left of Form Filled. Each one moves on an event your webinar platform already sends (the WebinarGeek webhook names are shown; Zoom's are webinar.registration_created and participant_joined):

    • Registered, tag registered: new registration
    • Attended, tag attended: new live viewer
    • No-Show, tag no-show: no show (it fires after the broadcast ends)
    • Replay Watched, tag replay-watched: new replay viewer

    Stage 3 already sets these tags. Here you only map each tag to a stage. Count attendance by the platform's live-viewer event, not by minutes watched.

    Capture Needed

    The pipeline editor with Registered / Attended / No-Show / Replay Watched added before Form Filled (GoHighLevel: Opportunities → Pipelines → Edit).

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  2. 2
    Point the Offer Button at Two Doors

    The offer button, the chat link and the replay email all use one link ending in ?src=live, so every deal remembers it came from the session.

    • High-ticket offers: the link opens the booking page (Form Filled, then the shared chain).
    • Offers below roughly a thousand: it opens a checkout, and a paid order jumps straight to Payment Completed with the tag purchased.

    Anyone who answers "yes" to the discovery-call poll (field poll_4_answer) gets a personal booking message within the hour.

    Capture Needed

    A booking page or checkout opened from the offer link with ?src=live in the address bar (the reader's own tool).

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  3. 3
    Keep Session No-Shows Out of the Sales Chain

    Someone who missed the live session is tagged no-show and gets Stage 3's replay emails. Someone who misses a booked sales call is tagged call-no-show and gets this stage's recovery. They're different people with different messages. Never let one tag do both jobs.

    Capture Needed

    A contact record showing both the `no-show` (session) and `call-no-show` (sales call) tags as separate tags.

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

S5 · Revenue & Deal PipelineReverse Squeeze Page (VSL)

Pipeline Changes for a Reverse Squeeze Page

No date and no clock: watch depth and a score band decide the stage, and two prices share one pipeline.

1The Full Setup
2The Task

Replace the event stages with depth stages: how far someone got through Part 1 decides what happens next, never the calendar. The bridge opt-in is where they become registered, Part 2 follows at once, and the application's score band routes them: top to the booked-call chain, middle to a lower-ticket checkout, bottom to long-term follow-up. You're done when the depth events land on a real test contact and each band reaches its next stage.

Steps
4
Examples
2
Runs On
Wistia · Dodo Payments
3Step by Step
  1. 1
    Add the Depth Stages

    Add VSL Started (event vsl_play; start the field max_depth_pct), then tag depth as they watch: depth-25, depth-50 and depth-75. Nurture follows the band, never a clock:

    • Under 25%: wrong person or wrong hook. One re-engage, then let them go.
    • 25–75%: interested but interrupted. Send the missing piece.
    • Past the Threshold (depth-75, event vsl_progress_75): show the Part 2 bridge.

    Keep the threshold in your spec. The playbook starts it at three-quarters through Part 1.

    Capture Needed

    The video host's engagement/heatmap view or the CRM contact timeline showing the depth-25/50/75 tags.

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  2. 2
    Make the Bridge Opt-In Your Registration

    There's no registration form up front. The bridge form ("Part 2 goes deeper. Where do I send it?") is where the contact gets the canonical registered tag. Submitting it delivers Part 2 at once, on a page plus a backup email. Every event carries utm_*, landing_variant and vsl_cut, so you can tell which cut and page earned the opt-in.

    Capture Needed

    The opt-in bridge form appearing over the Part 1 page past the threshold.

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  3. 3
    Route by Score Band, Not by Date

    The application writes score_band as top, middle or bottom, using the bands and rule written in your spec (no numbers here; the sources disagree on thresholds):

    • Top goes to Eval Call Scheduled, the full shared chain, with No Show and all.
    • Middle goes to a self-serve, lower-ticket checkout, straight to Payment Completed.
    • Bottom goes to long-term follow-up, the 52-week engine.

    On the premium branch the canonical tags mean the call: attended = call held, no-show = call missed, purchased = paid.

    Capture Needed

    A workflow If/Else branch splitting on the score_band field (GoHighLevel: Automation → Workflows → If/Else).

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  4. 4
    Stop the Clock

    The timed reminder engine (the playbook's automation 8) has nothing to count down to here, so switch it off for this pipeline. Nurture fires per person, on depth. Reminders still apply to booked calls on the top-band branch.

    Capture Needed

    The reminder workflow shown as paused/disabled for the RSP pipeline (GoHighLevel: Automation → Workflows → Draft/Publish toggle).

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

The Route Sprint: A Plan That Holds Before the Trucks Leave, in 30 Days

We apply the ROUTE Method to two of your depots, with your data, alongside your planners.

Who It's for, and Who It Isn't

A fit if

You run 200–1,000-person distribution, cost per stop is on this quarter's agenda, and you can give us a planner for two hours a week.

Not a fit if

You're mid-way through a planning-system migration, or you run fewer than five vans.

What You Get

A costed baseline

Cost per stop by depot, customer and service level, from your own data.

Rebuilt routes for two depots

Load minimums, planned waves and premium slots only where they're paid for.

Dispatch guardrails

Budget alerts and dispatch rules switched on and tested.

The Dispatch Script Pack

The scripts your dispatchers use to explain the new plan to drivers and customers.

How It Works

1Weeks 1–2 · See

Connect the data, tag every route, agree the baseline with finance.

2Weeks 3–4 · Control

Rebuild routes for two depots and run them side by side with the old plan.

3Week 5 onward · Guard

Switch on alerts and rules, hand over the playbook, decide on the next depots.

S5 · Revenue & Deal PipelineChallenge

Pipeline Changes for a Challenge

Two closes: a paid entry before Day 1, then the ascension offer to people who already paid once.

1The Full Setup
2The Task

Put registration, the paid entry, the intake and each day's attendance in front of Form Filled, so the pipeline shows who is still with you when the ascension offer lands on the last day. The entry payment is tagged entry-purchased and treated as a filter; purchased is kept for the ascension. You're done when a test buyer moves through Entry Purchased and each day on its own, and the ascension offer routes to the booked-call chain or a checkout.

Steps
3
Examples
2
Runs On
Dodo Payments · Claude Code
3Step by Step
  1. 1
    Add Registered, Entry Purchased and Intake

    Add three columns in front of Form Filled:

    • Registered: tag registered, plus the field lane (free or paid) from the form.
    • Entry Purchased: tag entry-purchased, from the verified payment webhook. Its metadata carries the lane and the UTMs.
    • Intake Submitted: from the intake survey.

    Keep purchased for the ascension, so you can see who bought twice.

    Capture Needed

    The pipeline editor with Registered / Entry Purchased / Intake Submitted added before Form Filled.

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  2. 2
    Add One Stage per Day, and the Daily Loop

    For each day, add Day N Attended (tags attended-day-1 … attended-day-3, and no-show-day-N for a miss), moved by the live platform's participant-join event. Today only a Join-button click (session_join) is captured; true attendance tracking is planned.

    A challenge adds a ninth automation to the playbook's eight: survey submitted → the AI generates the day's output → PDF and link delivered (survey_submitted_day{N}, then output_delivered_day{N}). It is the product, and it is planned in our own build. Log each delivery, so a missing output shows up as a stuck stage. Someone who doesn't finish Day 2 is the early warning: chase them the same evening.

    Capture Needed

    The contact timeline showing attended-day-N and a daily output-delivered event (planned: T-024/T-032/T-033).

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  3. 3
    Make the Last Day the Close

    The ascension offer lands on the last day, sold to people who paid once and saw the method work. High-ticket offers go to apply or book a call (Form Filled, then the shared chain). Offers they can buy on the spot go straight to Ascended, tagged purchased.

    Everyone who doesn't ascend goes to Stage 6, split by how far they got:

    • attended every day → ascension follow-up
    • dropped after Day 1 or 2 → recordings and a catch-up
    • never attended → replay and the next cohort
    • entry buyers who didn't ascend → the offer for a set window, then the long-term track
    Capture Needed

    The final-day offer link opening a booking page or checkout (the reader's own tool).

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

S5 · Revenue & Deal Pipeline

Reminders and Follow-Ups for Every Stage

One sequence per stage, each with its own clock, channel and exit, generated from your survey answers.

1The Full Setup
2The Task

Give every pipeline stage its own sequence: what fires automatically, what a person does, how fast, and where the contact goes if nothing happens. Generate the words from your Day 1 and Day 2 survey answers so every message sounds like you and names your offer, then load them into your CRM. You're done when every stage in your pipeline has a sequence with an exit condition, and a reply or a booking stops it.

Steps
6
Examples
11
Runs On
Google Calendar · Twilio · Gmail · Dodo Payments · Claude Code
3Step by Step
  1. 1
    Put a Clock on Every Stage

    Copy this matrix into your spec. Each line is one sequence:

    • Enquiry: an acknowledgement email with the booking link and an SMS at once. A call within 5 minutes during working hours, then a call a day for 3 days (day 2 adds an SMS with three slots).
    • Form filled, no booking: reviewed within 12 hours. Qualified leads get a call to book; unreachable ones get the calendar link.
    • Call booked: confirmation email and SMS at once, then reminders 48 hours, 24 hours and 1 hour before.
    • No show: an SMS with new slots inside 5 minutes, an email inside 15, two calls the same day, then the 7-day workflow.
    • Follow-up: a recap email the same day; follow-ups weekly for high intent, every two weeks for medium.
    • Proposal sent: a follow-up at 48 hours and at 7 days, plus a call when it's opened.
    • Invoice sent: reminders 3 days before, on the due date, and 3 and 7 days late.
    • Paid: the welcome email at once, and kickoff booked within 3–7 business days.
    • Lost: a door-open email, a reason code and a re-engage date.
  2. 2
    Generate Your Templates From Your Survey

    Open your survey page and click Copy answers (or Download my answers). Open Claude Code in your workshop folder, paste the Generate Every Follow-Up prompt below, and paste your answers where it says so.

    It writes one file per stage into follow-ups/. Each file holds the email, SMS and WhatsApp versions, the send offsets and the exit condition, using your offer, your call name, your prep question and your channels. Read every file once. Anything that doesn't sound like you, tell it why, and it fixes it.

    Tip It only uses channels you ticked in the survey. No SMS consent means no SMS step, and it says so in the file.

    Capture Needed

    Claude Code running the follow-up prompt and the generated follow-ups/ folder listing (Claude desktop app → Code tab).

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  3. 3
    Build the Booked-Call Reminders First

    If you build only one sequence today, build this one: a booked call with no reminders is a coin flip. The trigger is a booking created. The steps are a confirmation email and SMS, a wait until 48 hours before, an email, a wait until 24 hours before, an email and SMS, a wait until 1 hour before, and an SMS.

    Put a reschedule link in every message. A moved call beats a no-show.

  4. 4
    Build the No-Show Recovery

    The trigger is an appointment marked no-show, which also adds call-no-show. The sequence:

    1. SMS within 5 minutes with new slots.
    2. Email within 15 minutes: what they'd have got, plus the rebook link.
    3. A task for two call attempts the same day.
    4. The 7-day email, SMS and call workflow.
    5. Day 7 with no reply adds ghosted and hands them to the 52-week engine.

    A rebooking at any point cancels the workflow.

  5. 5
    Build Proposal and Invoice Follow-Ups

    Proposal watchdog: the trigger is the stage moving to Proposal Sent. Wait 48 hours; if there's no reply, send the email. Wait until day 7, then create a call task and send an offer of a 15-minute walkthrough. On the expiry date, extend once or close it as lost (timing).

    Invoice reminders: the trigger is the invoice being sent. Remind 3 days before the due date, on it, then 3 and 7 days late. Payment moves the deal from the payment webhook, never from someone ticking a box.

  6. 6
    Make Every Sequence Stop When People Act

    Set one exit rule on every sequence: a reply, a booking or a stage change removes the contact. Nobody should get a no-show text after they've rebooked, or an invoice reminder after they've paid. Test each exit once with a test contact before you switch the sequence on.

Generate Every Follow-Up From Your Survey Answers
You are my revenue-operations writer. Using ONLY the facts in my survey answers below, write the follow-up templates for every stage of my sales pipeline.

My pipeline (11 stages + a No Show exit): Form Filled → Eval Call Scheduled (No Show exit) → Qualified / Unqualified → Sales Call Held → Follow-Up → Proposal Sent → Proposal Accepted → Payment Completed → Onboarding → Delivery.

Use these facts from my answers:
- Day 1: who I sell to, who signs and what they are measured on, the objection that kills deals, my offer sentence, my offer block (price, guarantee, what is and isn't included), my brand voice (use the 3 adjectives, avoid the 3 "not" adjectives), my mechanism and its steps, my strongest proof.
- Day 2: my funnel shape / mechanism, the missing link in my close chain, who works each stage, how my offer closes, which follow-up channels I may use, my call's name and prep question, my follow-up rules (no-show, proposal expiry, "not now"), which extra pipelines I'm running.

Write one markdown file per sequence into a folder called follow-ups/:
01-enquiry.md · 02-form-no-booking.md · 03-call-reminders.md · 04-no-show-recovery.md · 05-post-call-recap.md · 06-follow-up.md · 07-proposal-watchdog.md · 08-invoice-reminders.md · 09-welcome-onboarding.md · 10-deal-lost.md · 11-nurture-check-in.md
plus one file per extra pipeline I chose (no-show recovery, nurture-back, referral & expansion, re-engagement).

Each file must contain:
1. Trigger (the event that starts it) and exit (what stops it: a reply, a booking or a stage change).
2. A table of steps: offset (e.g. +5 min, T−24h, day 3), channel, owner (automation or which role), purpose.
3. The full copy for every step, per channel: email (subject, preheader, body), SMS (one segment: 160 characters in plain text, 70 if it contains an emoji), WhatsApp (under 400 characters; mark it "needs approved template" if it's business-initiated), and a call script of 3–5 lines for call steps.
4. Personalisation fields in {curly_braces}: {first_name}, {booking_link}, {meeting_link}, {reschedule_link}, {invoice_number}, {amount}, {due_date}, {payment_link}, {expiry_date}.

Rules:
- Only use channels I ticked. If I didn't tick SMS, write no SMS steps and say why at the top of the file.
- Use my call's name and my prep question in the booking and reminder messages.
- Use my proposal expiry and "not now" timing exactly as I wrote them.
- No invented numbers, results, testimonials or client names. If a message needs proof, use my strongest proof exactly as written, or leave {proof} as a placeholder.
- Sound like my brand voice. Short sentences. No hype words.

When you're done, print a one-line summary per file, then ask me which file I want to review first.

MY SURVEY ANSWERS:
<paste your Day 1 and Day 2 answers here>

S5 · Revenue & Deal Pipeline

The Four Extra Pipelines

No-show recovery, nurture-back, referrals and re-engagement, each ending back in the main pipeline.

1The Full Setup
2The Task

Build four small pipelines beside the main one, so the people it would otherwise forget are tracked like deals: missed calls, the "not now"s, happy customers who could refer, and contacts who've gone quiet. Each has its own few stages, one owner and one way back into the main pipeline. You're done when each extra pipeline has an entry trigger, a weekly review, and an exit that lands in the main pipeline or the 52-week engine.

Steps
5
Examples
7
Runs On
Gmail · GoHighLevel
3Step by Step
  1. 1
    No-Show Recovery: Missed → Rebooked or Ghosted

    Stages: Missed → Rebook Offered → Rebooked | Ghosted.

    • Enters: the tag call-no-show.
    • Runs: the recovery sequence (SMS in 5 minutes, email in 15, two calls the same day, then 7 days of mixed touches).
    • Leaves: Rebooked returns to the main pipeline at Eval Call Scheduled. Silent at day 7 is tagged ghosted and moves to the 52-week engine.

    A booked call you lose is still a warm lead.

  2. 2
    Nurture-Back: For Every "Not Now"

    Stages: Parked → Warming → Check-In Call → Back in Pipeline | Stay Parked.

    • Enters: the tag nurture, or a lost deal with the reason "timing". Set reengage_after to the date they gave you.
    • Warming: they opened or clicked something in the last 30 days, or reengage_after has arrived.
    • Check-In Call: a short, personal note or call. Quarterly at most while they stay parked.
    • Leaves: ready goes back to Form Filled or Eval Call Scheduled.

    Unqualified today isn't unqualified forever.

  3. 3
    Referral and Expansion: Ask at the High Point

    Stages: Advocate Identified → Ask Made → Intro Received → Referral Booked, with a side branch Upsell Proposed → Won.

    • Enters: a customer in Delivery gives a positive check-in or tells you about a result.
    • Ask Made: ask for one specific kind of person and offer a two-line intro they can forward.
    • Leaves: referred leads enter the main pipeline tagged referral, so you can see what advocates are worth. Expansion work is proposed to existing customers here, before you chase new ones.

    Advocates are the cheapest acquisition channel you have.

  4. 4
    Re-Engagement: The Nine-Word Email

    Stages: Dormant → Nine-Word Email Sent → Replied | Silent → Reactivated | Suppressed.

    • Enters: no opens in 90 days (or an old list you never followed up).
    • The email: a first-name subject and one plain question, e.g. "Are you still interested in {result_metric} for {company_name}?". A/B test it against an AI-personalised version that names one detail from their record.
    • Leaves: any reply is tagged reactivated and goes back to the main pipeline. Ten unopened sends means suppressed, and they drop to a lower send frequency. Let people leave quietly.
  5. 5
    Review All Four Once a Week

    Give each extra pipeline one owner and fifteen minutes a week. Look for three things: cards with no next-action date, cards that haven't moved in two weeks, and anyone who replied but was never answered. Every extra pipeline ends by handing back to the main pipeline or to the 52-week engine. None of them is a dead end.

S5 · Revenue & Deal Pipeline

Set It Up in GoHighLevel

Path A: fields, tags, five pipelines, the booking calendar and the workflows, all inside GoHighLevel.

1The Full Setup
2The Task

Build the whole of Stage 5 inside GoHighLevel: the fields and tags, the Sales pipeline with its eleven stages and No Show exit, the four extra pipelines, a booking calendar with its reminders, and the workflows that move deals and send follow-ups on their own. Paste in the copy you generated from your survey. You're done when a test contact books, misses, rebooks and pays, and every stage move and message happens without you.

Steps
9
Examples
4
Runs On
GoHighLevel · Google Calendar · Twilio
3Step by Step
  1. 1
    Start From a Clean Sub-Account

    Do the build in its own sub-account, so test contacts and workflows never mix with anything live. If your agency already has a pipeline snapshot you trust, open Account Snapshots in the agency view and create the sub-account from it, then check every stage and field against this guide. Otherwise start empty. It takes less time than untangling someone else's stages.

  2. 2
    Create the Custom Fields

    Go to Settings → Custom Fields, choose the Contact object and click Create field. Create each field from the fields list in The 11-Stage Deal Pipeline, with exactly those names: source, the four UTMs, mechanism (dropdown), diagnostic_score (number), score_band (dropdown), priority (dropdown P1–P3), owner, next_action_date (date).

    Then switch the object to Opportunity and create the deal fields: deal_value, proposal_sent_at, proposal_expires_at, lost_reason (dropdown), reengage_after.

  3. 3
    Create the Tags

    Tags are created the first time you type them. Open Contacts, tick your test contact, click the Add Tag icon and type each tag once: registered, attended, no-show, purchased, replay-watched, call-no-show, enquiry, ghosted, nurture, deal-lost, referral, reactivated. Spell them exactly like this; every workflow matches on the text.

  4. 4
    Build the Sales Pipeline and the Four Extra Pipelines

    Go to Opportunities → Pipelines → Create new pipeline. Name it Sales and add the stages in order: Form Filled, Eval Call Scheduled, No Show, Qualified, Unqualified, Sales Call Held, Follow-Up, Proposal Sent, Proposal Accepted, Payment Completed, Onboarding, Delivery. Use the arrows to reorder and Add stage for each one.

    Give the two exits (No Show, Unqualified) a stage colour so they stand out on the board. Then create four more pipelines the same way: No-Show Recovery, Nurture-Back, Referral and Expansion, Re-Engagement, with the stages listed in The Four Extra Pipelines.

  5. 5
    Set Up the Booking Calendar and Its Reminders

    Go to Settings → Calendars, open your sales-call calendar with Edit, then Notifications. Turn on the booking confirmation for the contact on Email and SMS, and add reminders at 48 hours, 24 hours and 1 hour before the appointment. Paste in your generated copy from follow-ups/03-call-reminders.md.

    Add your prep question as a required question on the booking form, so it lands on the contact before the call.

  6. 6
    Wire Tag to Stage

    This is automation 6: tags and events move deals, people don't. Go to Automation → Workflows → Create Workflow. Build one small workflow per move, for example:

    • Trigger: Customer Booked Appointment. Action: Create/Update Opportunity → Sales → Eval Call Scheduled.
    • Trigger: Appointment Status = Showed. Action: update the opportunity to Sales Call Held.
    • Trigger: Contact Tag added purchased. Action: update the opportunity to Payment Completed.

    Turn on Allow Opportunity to Move in the action, or the card stays where it is.

  7. 7
    Build the No-Show and Follow-Up Workflows

    One workflow per sequence in your follow-ups/ folder. For the no-show:

    1. Trigger: Appointment Status = No Show.
    2. Actions: add tag call-no-show, move to No Show, Send SMS (your 5-minute text), Wait 10 minutes, Send Email, create two call tasks, then the 7-day steps with Wait between them.
    3. Goal: Customer Booked Appointment, so a rebooking ends the workflow.

    Build the proposal watchdog the same way, with Pipeline Stage Changed → Proposal Sent as the trigger and waits of 48 hours and 7 days.

  8. 8
    Catch Deals That Stop Moving

    Add one more workflow with the Stale Opportunities trigger, filtered to the Sales pipeline, with Duration in days set to 7. The action is a task for the coordinator: "Stuck in stage: decide the next action or close it". It's the 7-day Follow-Up rule, enforced by the system instead of by memory.

  9. 9
    Walk a Test Contact Through the Board

    Open Opportunities and add a test contact through your real booking link. Watch the card: Eval Call Scheduled, then mark the appointment no-show and see it jump to No Show with the tag and the text sent. Rebook, mark it showed, move it through a proposal, and pay with a test payment. If you had to drag a card at any point, that move still needs its workflow.

S5 · Revenue & Deal Pipeline

Set It Up With the Starter CRM and Claude Code

Path B: a small CRM you run from a folder; Claude Code connects your forms, calendar, payments and messages.

1The Full Setup
2The Task

Run your pipeline from a folder on your own computer instead of a subscription CRM. The starter CRM already stores contacts, records events and moves deals through the eleven stages on its own. You paste six prompts into Claude Code to connect your form, calendar, payments and messages. You're done when a real booking and a test payment move a contact through the pipeline and its follow-ups send without you.

Steps
6
Examples
3
Runs On
Cal.com · Dodo Payments · Claude Code · GitHub · Resend · Twilio
3Step by Step
  1. 1
    Get the Starter CRM

    Download the folder: crm-starter.zip ↗. Unzip it into your workshop folder and open a terminal there. Inside:

    • pipeline.json: the eleven stages, the No Show exit, the entry event for each, and the front stages for your mechanism
    • fields.json: the tags and fields, with the same names as every other guide
    • crm.py: the core, with no installs needed (Python 3 only)
    • prompts/: the six Claude Code prompts that connect it to your tools

    The README's status table says honestly what's built and what you build with the prompts.

  2. 2
    Walk a Test Contact Through It

    Run these one at a time:

    1. python3 crm.py init
    2. python3 crm.py add you@example.com --mechanism webinar
    3. python3 crm.py event you@example.com form.submitted
    4. python3 crm.py event you@example.com booking.created
    5. python3 crm.py event you@example.com booking.no_show
    6. python3 crm.py board

    The deal is in No Show with the call-no-show tag, and you never moved it. Tools report events; events move deals. That's the whole design.

  3. 3
    Connect Your Forms and Calendar (Prompt 01)

    Open Claude Code in the crm-starter folder and paste prompts/01-intake.md. Fill in the two tool names it asks for. Claude reads the folder, finds your tools' API docs, asks you to put each key in .env (never in the chat), and builds intake.py, which checks for new submissions and bookings every 5 minutes.

    It polls rather than waiting for webhooks, because a CRM on your own machine can't be reached from the internet.

    Tip Keys go in .env, which is already git-ignored. Never paste a key into a prompt.

    Capture Needed

    Claude Code open in crm-starter with prompt 01 pasted, reading README.md and pipeline.json.

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  4. 4
    Connect Payments (Prompt 02)

    Paste prompts/02-payments.md and name your payment provider. Claude builds payments.py, which confirms each payment with the provider's own API, never with the browser, and records payment.succeeded. The CRM adds purchased and moves the deal to Payment Completed. Prove it with one test-mode payment.

    Capture Needed

    Planned: payments.py is built by the reader with prompt 02, so there is nothing to capture until it exists. Capture crm.py show after a test-mode payment.

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  5. 5
    Start the Follow-Ups (Prompt 03)

    This one needs the follow-ups/ folder you generated in Reminders and Follow-Ups for Every Stage. Paste prompts/03-follow-up-runner.md. Claude builds runner.py, which schedules each stage's steps when a deal enters it, cancels them when the person replies, books or moves on, and sends what's due every 5 minutes by email, SMS or WhatsApp, only on channels they agreed to.

    Run python3 runner.py --dry-run and read the next 24 hours of messages before you switch real sending on.

    Capture Needed

    Planned: runner.py is built by the reader with prompt 03. Capture its --dry-run output for a test contact.

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  6. 6
    Add the Extra Pipelines, a Board and a Schedule (Prompts 04–06)
    • 04 adds the four extra pipelines next to Sales.
    • 05 builds a local board at http://localhost:8765, with columns in pipeline order and one card per deal.
    • 06 makes intake, payments and the runner run every 5 minutes on their own, and writes a daily 08:00 summary of new leads, moves, sends and anything stuck.

    When all six are done, update the README's status table. Nothing in this setup depends on a third-party automation platform.

    Capture Needed

    Planned: the board is built by the reader with prompt 05. Capture it at localhost:8765 with test deals.

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

Read README.md, pipeline.json, fields.json, schema.sql and crm.py in this folder.
Then explain back to me in plain words, in under 150 words:
1. How a contact moves from one stage to the next (which events do it).
2. What is BUILT today and what I still build with the prompts in prompts/.
3. Which of prompts 01–06 I should run first, given that my mechanism is <webinar | reverse squeeze page | challenge>, my offer closes by <booked call | checkout | both>, and my tools are <form tool>, <booking tool>, <payment provider>, <email provider>.
Don't change any files yet.

S6

Stage 6 of 6

52-Week Growth Engine

S6 — What Happens to Everyone Who Didn't Buy

Most of your list, on any given cycle, will not buy. That is normal and it is not failure — it's timing. The mistake is letting them go quiet, because a warm list that goes silent for six months is a cold list again.

Most of your list, on any cycle, won't buy yet. Stage 6 keeps them warm for a year: one weekly email that teaches your method a step at a time and proves it with stories, a short WhatsApp message beside every email, and a rare SMS when something is time-critical. The newsletter is drafted by an AI every week from your own context and that week's news; you edit, approve and schedule it. Everyone enters through one tag, and anyone who replies re-enters the pipeline.

◆ Do this · define the four tags now and never rename them

registered · attended · no-show · purchased. Every automation, every report and every audience you build for the rest of the year keys off these four. Name them today, write them into the spec, and treat renaming one as a breaking change — because it is.

The Weekly NewsletterThe WhatsApp Twin of Every EmailThe SMS NudgeThe AI Newsletter: A Weekly Draft in Your Claude Code

S6 · 52-Week Growth Engine

The Weekly Newsletter

A welcome series that teaches your method step by step, then a weekly letter on a 12-topic rotation.

1The Full Setup
2The Task

Build the email side of the 52-week engine. Everyone who finishes without buying gets a welcome series that teaches your method one step at a time and proves it with case studies and tool how-tos, then a weekly letter on a 12-topic rotation. It lives in Beehiiv (or your email tool), enters through one tag, and sends people who reply back to the pipeline. You're done when the series is written, the automation is live, and the first weekly letter is scheduled.

Steps
7
Examples
11
Runs On
Beehiiv · GoHighLevel

How This Changes by Mechanism

The series walks through the steps you taught in the session, so Email 1 can say "you saw the overview live; here's each step in depth".

3Step by Step
  1. 1
    One Entry Tag, Four Segments

    Everyone enters through one tag, from Stage 3 or Stage 5: finished the event without buying, lost with a "not now", or ghosted. Inside the letter, keep four segments apart:

    • Non-buyers: the biggest group. Keep teaching, and re-invite them each cycle.
    • Buyers: onboarding first, then the next rung up.
    • Lapsed: one reactivation offer, then less often.
    • Advocates: ask for referrals and reviews.

    In Beehiiv, a tag per segment is enough. Create them under Audience → Subscribers → Tags.

  2. 2
    Write Email 1: The Roadmap

    The first email thanks them for coming and lists every step of your method that the series will walk through, one line each. It turns a list of emails into a course they want to finish.

    • Subject: the outcome, not the event. Preheader: the promise of the steps.
    • Body: thanks, the problem the series solves, the numbered steps, and "I'll walk you through each one in the next emails."
    • Sign-off: your first name. Rotate sign-offs across the series.
  3. 3
    Rotate Three Kinds of Email

    After Email 1, repeat this rotation until every step is covered:

    1. Step email: "(Step N/total)" in the subject. One idea, one task for the week, 4–5 questions to answer, a reply prompt, and a P.S. teasing the next step.
    2. Case study: Who? · Problem · Solution · Did it work? Then one call to book. Only results the customer approved in writing.
    3. Tool how-to: a practical walkthrough of one tool or tactic. Send a text version and a version with an image, and keep the one that gets more clicks.

    After the last step: one mindset email, then two templates they can use (an event template, an outreach template), then the weekly letter.

    Tip Write the whole series in one sitting from your mechanism's steps (Day 1). The AI newsletter guide below drafts it for you.

  4. 4
    Build the Series as a Beehiiv Automation

    Go to Audience → Automations → New automation. Pick the trigger Signed up (or Segment action if people arrive by tag from your CRM), then add an email step and a time delay for each email in the series, in order. Activate the trigger when the last email is in.

    Test the cadence for the first month: send one group daily, one every 2 days and one every 3 days, then keep the winner for everyone.

  5. 5
    Then the Weekly Letter: The 12-Topic Rotation

    Once the series ends, send one letter a week. What it's about comes from the playbook's 12-topic rotation: one theme per month, six kinds of theme, run twice a year:

    1. the problem, restated
    2. your mechanism, one step
    3. a customer story
    4. a common mistake
    5. a tool or template
    6. an invitation back in

    Every weekly letter that month goes deeper on the month's theme, and the WhatsApp and SMS twins reuse it. Keep a rough ratio of four useful sends for every one that asks for something.

  6. 6
    Let People Leave Quietly

    Remove anyone after 20 unopened emails. A list that never opens hurts delivery for the people who do. Put a visible unsubscribe and a "less often" option in every footer.

    For an old list you never followed up, run the reactivation series first: a nine-word email ("Are you still interested in {result_metric}?") A/B tested against an AI-personalised one. Anyone who opens joins the welcome series; anyone silent after 10 sends is removed.

    Capture Needed

    beehiiv segment or automation condition for unengaged subscribers.

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  7. 7
    Schedule Each Letter Into Its Slot

    Pick one day and time and never move it, so readers learn when to expect you. In the post flow, go to Review → Schedule → Schedule for later, set the date and time, and confirm. The button changes to show the scheduled time. The AI newsletter guide below drafts each letter a day or two before this slot.

Northwind Newsletter: The 52-Week Roadmap

One story told across a year for Heads of Operations: four phases, six pillars, and a CTA that firms up as the reader does.

Weekly from Maya Okonkwo · checkpoints at weeks 12, 26, 39 and 52

Who Reads It

A Head of Operations at a 200–1,000-person mid-market distribution business. They already feel it: replanning routes by hand every morning, late deliveries nobody can price, and a routing conversation they know they need to have but haven't started with confidence.

Six Editorial Pillars (Every Issue Maps to One)

The replan problem · Awareness

The morning scramble, named precisely enough that the reader feels understood.

The ROUTE Method · Consideration

What each step changes on an ordinary Tuesday, walked through one step at a time.

Proof from real networks · Consideration → decision

a regional distributor, introduced in two parts across the year. Every outcome is Result metric.

The path · Decision → purchase

How a rollout actually runs: first depot, first owner, first number.

The market · Awareness → consideration

Carrier costs, delivery windows, a carrier announcing new surcharges, read for what they mean to the plan.

The people · Trust at every stage

Maya Okonkwo and the team: how we think, what we won't do, who we've worked alongside.

(Step 2/8) Find the capacity that's doing nothingInbox
Preview text A van a third full costs the same to run as a full one
MO
Maya OkonkwoUnsubscribe10:00 AM
to me ▾

Hi Sam,

Someone at the session put it better than I ever have: half our vans leave the yard looking busy and come back having done a morning's work.

That's step two, and it's usually the biggest single line in the teardown.

Export 07 gives you fill at departure, by weight and by volume, plus engine-on idle time. Whichever of weight or volume is higher tells you how full the vehicle really was while you paid for it.

"Underused" is a word people argue about, so we don't use words. We use the thresholds set in Export 01:

  • Average fill below 50%
  • Even its busiest day below 70%
  • Idle time above 45 minutes a shift
  • Only routes that ran at least 20 times in the window
  • Only vehicles that cost more than a set floor over the 90 days

Read that as a sentence: a vehicle that ran its route at least twenty times, cost real money, averaged under half full and never broke 70% even on its best day is not busy. It's oversized, or it's one route too many. The last two thresholds are there so you don't lose a week arguing about a van that ran twice.

Why the busiest-day figure matters: an average gets fooled by one peak. A route that averages 45% because it's rammed on Mondays and empty the rest of the week is a different problem from one that never passes 55%. The first needs a different schedule. The second needs a smaller vehicle, or a merge.

Your task this week: run Export 07, apply the five thresholds, and produce one list: route, vehicle, average fill, busiest-day fill, idle minutes, and the 90-day cost from your baseline. Sort by cost, highest first.

In my experience the top ten rows of that list hold a large share of everything you could save. Before any new software. Before any fleet decision. Just from seeing it.

Which do you think you have more of: vehicles that are the wrong size, or routes that are the right size but run on days nobody needs them? Reply with your instinct, and I'll tell you what the data usually says.

More next week,

Maya

P.S. Step 3 is the second answer, and it's more common than people expect.

💬🎥
Why it works

Replaces an arguable word ('underused') with five explicit thresholds; the P.S. opens the loop the next step closes.

Preview text The real story behind the eight steps
MO
Maya Okonkwo10:00 AM
to me ▾

Hi Sam,

For six months I've shown you the method. Today, where it came from.

WHO: Me. Maya Okonkwo, Founder of Northwind. Before there was a Northwind, I ran the dispatch office at a distributor not unlike yours.

THE PROBLEM: Every morning I rebuilt the day's routes by hand. The plan was ready at 6:40, the first truck left at 7:00, and by 9:00 the plan had fallen apart: a customer's dock was closed, a driver was out, an order had been added by phone. My phone rang all day. Cost went up every quarter, and when finance asked me why, I honestly couldn't say which route, which depot or which decision was doing it. I was the system, and the system was tired.

THE SOLUTION: Before I sold this to anyone, I ran it on my own operation. The first version of the teardown was a spreadsheet and three exports I pulled on a Sunday.

HOW IT WENT, IN THREE PHASES:

  • See it. The baseline replaced the monthly argument about where the money went. For the first time, every stop had a cost and every cost had a route.
  • Move it. Sorting the routes replaced the morning replan. The biggest surprise was the RETIRE pile: standing routes nobody could explain.
  • Keep it. One page, six numbers, every month, replaced the quarterly panic.

THE HONEST PART: Most of what I tried first didn't work. My first plan was beautiful and ignored receiving windows, and the drivers quietly ignored it for a month. My first ownership rule named a team inbox; nobody answered it. The side-by-side check exists because I once switched a depot over on a Friday and spent the weekend apologising to customers. Every one of those failures is a step in the method now.

DID IT WORK? Result metric. Social proof.

THE KEY INSIGHT: I stopped looking for the one clever fix and started building something that ran without me standing in the dispatch office at 6am.

WHAT CHANGED IN MY HEAD:

  • A number I can't take apart isn't a number; it's a mood.
  • Settings beat heroics.
  • Every route needs a name next to it.
  • Measure the saving exactly the way you measured the cost.

So, Sam: do you want a plan that holds before the trucks leave, without it depending on you being in early every morning?

If you do, let's map your operation together. 30 minutes, your own routes on the screen, and you leave with the first three things to change: cal.example/northwind/call

Maya Okonkwo
Founder, Northwind

P.S. Tomorrow's email is the last one in the series, and it gives you both ways forward.

The method applied first to the person selling it; the failures are the credibility, so they stay in.

Hey Sam,

That's the series. Thank you for reading it; genuinely, the replies have been some of the best conversations I've had this year.

Here's where you stand.

Steps 1 to 4, the entire teardown, are yours. The exports are published, the thresholds are in your inbox, and none of it needs us. Plenty of teams run it, act on it and never speak to me. That's a good outcome, and it's why we publish it.

Steps 5 to 8 are harder. Not to understand (you've read them, and they aren't complicated) but to own. Someone has to hold the switchover calendar, negotiate with depot managers, keep the side-by-side plans honest, and still be reporting the number a year from now when it's nobody's favourite project.

Some teams have that person. If you do, you have everything you need from this series, and I'd honestly rather you just went and did it.

If you don't, that's the job we do.

TWO DOORS

Door 1, do it yourself: every export, every threshold, no form: northwind.example/calculator

Door 2, do it with us: 30 minutes where we run the teardown on your operation live, go through the findings together, and you leave with a ranked list of where your delivery money is going: cal.example/northwind/call

Nothing to prepare for the second one. Bring last month's route list.

One last thought. Nobody's job title is "reduce delivery cost." This work always sits on top of someone's real job, which is why it slips quarter after quarter while the number gets worse.

The way out isn't more discipline. It's making the first step small enough to start: one export, one number, one afternoon. The rest follows from having looked.

Thanks for reading.

Maya Okonkwo
Founder, Northwind

P.S. If the timing's wrong now but right in three months, just reply "three months" and I'll follow up then. It works more often than you'd think.

Maya OkonkwoUnsubscribe10:00 AM
to me ▾

Hi Sam,

Thanks for being at Plan Every Route Before 7am. I hope you left with at least one thing you could go and check before Monday's first truck leaves the yard.

We built that session around a problem nearly every Head of Operations recognises and very few can prove: delivery costs are climbing faster than volume, and nobody in the room can point at the route, the depot or the decision that's driving it.

Over the next few weeks I'm going to walk you through the whole ROUTE Method, the one we run on customer engagements. Not the highlights. The actual steps, with the actual exports we pull.

Here's the road ahead:

  • Step 1. Set a baseline you can defend: every stop with a cost attached to it.
  • Step 2. Find the idle capacity: vehicles leaving a third full and costing the same as full ones.
  • Step 3. Measure the premium-mode tax: overtime and same-day couriers doing work that was known days ago.
  • Step 4. Price the burn and the markup: failed deliveries, and two-person crews where one would do.
  • Step 5. Sort every route: Keep, Redesign, Retire, or Move to a cheaper mode.
  • Step 6. Move in waves, and prove the new plan in parallel before anyone switches over.
  • Step 7. Put a control tower on it so the savings don't quietly leak back.
  • Step 8. Prove the business case with numbers your finance director will sign.

Steps 1 to 4 you can run yourself this month; we publish every export and every threshold. Steps 5 to 8 are where most teams want a second pair of hands, and I'll tell you honestly which is which as we go.

One thing to say up front. The goal isn't a smaller fuel bill. It's getting back the capacity your fleet is spending on work nobody needed: the new depot, the extra delivery day, the customers you've been turning away. The savings are how you pay for them.

More next week.

Maya Okonkwo
Founder, Northwind

Lists all eight steps on day one: a reader who can see the whole map knows what's coming and stays for it.

The WhatsApp Twin of Every Email

One short WhatsApp beside each email: a nudge to open it, or the same idea in a few lines.

1The Full Setup
2The Task

Give every newsletter email a WhatsApp twin: either a pointer that makes the reader open the email, or the same idea in a few lines. Twins go only to people who opted in to WhatsApp, as approved message templates, an hour after the email. You're done when your first two twins are approved as templates and scheduled next to their emails.

Steps
5
Examples
2
Runs On
Beehiiv · WhatsApp · WATI
3Step by Step
  1. 1
    Choose Pointer or Compressed

    Decide per email:

    • Pointer: for long emails (step emails, tool how-tos). Their name, the hook from the subject, one line of the takeaway, and the link to the email's web version.
    • Compressed: for short emails (mindset, case studies). The one idea in 3–5 lines, ending with a question they can answer by replying.

    Either way it's one idea and one link. WhatsApp is read on a phone between other things.

    Capture Needed

    A pointer twin and a compressed twin side by side in a WhatsApp chat on a phone (the reader's own WhatsApp Business account).

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  2. 2
    Stay Inside WhatsApp's Limits

    The rules come from Meta's WhatsApp Business Platform:

    • Opt-in first. You may only message people who agreed to hear from you on WhatsApp. Add the tick box to your registration form.
    • Templates outside 24 hours. A message you start (not a reply) must be an approved template. Newsletter twins are the Marketing category.
    • Length. A template body can be up to 1,024 characters. Aim for under 400: a twin is a nudge, not a copy of the email.
    • Replies. When someone replies, a 24-hour window opens and you can answer freely, up to 4,096 characters per message.

    Sources: Meta: template components ↗ · Meta: getting opt-in ↗.

    Capture Needed

    WhatsApp Manager's template category notice.

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  3. 3
    Turn Each Twin Into a Template

    Write the twin with variables for the parts that change, {{1}} for the first name and {{2}} for the link, then submit it in WhatsApp Manager (or your provider's template screen). Meta checks the category. If it says the template will be marked as marketing, that's correct for a newsletter twin: submit it.

    Make the pointer version reusable, so one approved template covers every week and only the variables change.

  4. 4
    Send It an Hour After the Email

    Schedule the twin an hour after the email lands, never at the same minute, so the WhatsApp reminds them rather than competes. Use your WhatsApp Business provider's broadcast or campaign screen, or the follow-up runner from the starter CRM (it only sends to contacts with WhatsApp consent). Replies come to a real person and count as engagement in your CRM.

    Capture Needed

    A WhatsApp Business provider's broadcast/campaign scheduling screen with a send time set (the reader's own provider).

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  5. 5
    Generate the Twins With the Newsletter

    You don't write twins by hand. The AI newsletter's weekly task drafts the email and its WhatsApp twin together, checks the twin is under 400 characters, and marks which mode it used. You review both in the same place.

Write the WhatsApp Twin for an Email
Here is this week's newsletter email. Write its WhatsApp twin.

Rules:
- Choose POINTER if the email is over 250 words, otherwise COMPRESSED, and say which you chose.
- POINTER: line 1 = "Hi {{1}}," + the hook from the subject; line 2 = the one-line takeaway; line 3 = "Full thing in your inbox, or here: {{2}}".
- COMPRESSED: the single idea in 3–5 short lines, ending with a question they can answer by replying.
- Under 400 characters total (the hard limit for a template body is 1,024). Print the character count.
- My brand voice: <your three adjectives from Day 1>. No hype words, no more than one emoji.
- It will be sent as an approved Marketing template to people who opted in, an hour after the email.

The SMS Nudge

A one-segment text beside the emails that matter: invitations, deadlines and re-invites only.

1The Full Setup
2The Task

Add an SMS to the weeks that are time-critical (doors opening, a deadline, a live session), never to every letter. Each text is one segment, which is 160 characters of plain text or 70 once there's an emoji, and goes only to people who gave SMS consent. You're done when you have a pointer text and an invitation text ready, both under one segment, and your sender is set up.

Steps
4
Examples
1
Runs On
Beehiiv · Twilio
3Step by Step
  1. 1
    Decide Which Weeks Get a Text

    SMS is the rare rail. The playbook's cadence is email weekly, messaging fortnightly, and SMS only when it's time-critical. Text when:

    • a new cohort or event opens, or a seat deadline is close
    • a live session starts today
    • the "invitation back in" month of the rotation lands

    Every other week: no text. That's what keeps the texts that matter from being ignored.

    Capture Needed

    A content calendar with the SMS weeks marked (the reader's 52-week plan).

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  2. 2
    Fit It in One Segment

    A text over one segment is split and billed as several. The sizes, from Twilio's docs:

    • Plain text (GSM-7): 160 characters in one segment, 153 per segment once it splits.
    • Any emoji or non-GSM character (UCS-2): 70 in one segment, 67 per segment once it splits.

    One curly apostrophe can switch a whole text to the 70-character limit, so use straight quotes and no emoji. Source: Twilio: what is the SMS character limit? ↗

    Capture Needed

    An SMS composer showing the live character/segment counter (the reader's SMS provider).

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  3. 3
    Write the Two Texts You Need
    • Pointer: {brand}: new playbook on {topic} is in your inbox. 2-min read: {short_link}
    • Invitation: {brand}: {first_name}, doors open for {event_title} on {date}. Your seat: {short_link}. Reply STOP to opt out

    Start with who it's from, because people don't save your number. Use a short link. Include the opt-out wording where your country requires it.

    Capture Needed

    A drafted SMS in the provider's composer, with merge fields.

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  4. 4
    Send Only With Consent

    Only text people who ticked SMS consent on your form. In the starter CRM that's consent_sms, and the follow-up runner refuses to text anyone without it. In GoHighLevel, use a workflow Send SMS step filtered to contacts with your SMS-consent tag. Send in their daytime, an hour after the email.

Write the SMS for This Week
Here is this week's newsletter email and what's time-critical this week: <doors opening / deadline / live session / nothing>.

If nothing is time-critical, reply "No SMS this week" and stop.
Otherwise write ONE text:
- Starts with "<brand>:" so they know who it's from.
- One reason to act now, and the {short_link}.
- Plain GSM-7 characters only: straight quotes, no emoji, no em dashes.
- 160 characters maximum INCLUDING "Reply STOP to opt out" if my country needs it (<country>).
- Print the character count and confirm it's one segment.

The AI Newsletter: A Weekly Draft in Your Claude Code

Run one prompt once; every week Claude Code drafts your letter from your context and the news.

1The Full Setup
2The Task

Run one prompt in Claude Code, once, with your survey answers and a few inputs. It builds a folder holding everything it knows about your business and voice, writes your first draft on the spot, and creates a weekly task that drafts the next issue from that folder and the week's news in your field. Each week you give feedback, it revises and remembers the lesson, and you schedule the result in Beehiiv. You're done when the first draft is approved and scheduled, and the weekly task shows as active.

Steps
8
Examples
4
Runs On
Claude Code · Beehiiv
3Step by Step
  1. 1
    Open Claude Code in a New Folder

    Make a folder for the letter, e.g. weekly-letter. In the Claude desktop app, open the Code tab and start a session with that folder as the working folder. The desktop app matters: its scheduled tasks run on your computer with access to your files. Tasks created in the cloud can't see a local folder.

    Claude Code in a terminal works too: open the folder in a terminal and run claude. The setup prompt handles both.

    Capture Needed

    Claude desktop app → Code tab → new session with the weekly-letter folder selected as working folder.

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  2. 2
    Paste the Setup Prompt With Your Inputs

    Copy Set Up My AI Newsletter below. Fill in the inputs at the top:

    • the name
    • your send slot and a draft day one or two days earlier
    • the 3–5 topics you own and three sources you trust (your last survey answer has all of these)
    • whether your Beehiiv plan has the Create Post API
    • whether to install the schedule now

    Then paste your answers from the survey's Copy answers button and send it.

    Capture Needed

    The setup prompt pasted into a Claude Code session with the inputs filled in.

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  3. 3
    Check the Folder It Built

    It writes everything as plain files you can read and edit:

    • context/: your offer, audience, positioning and mechanism, quoted from your answers, with TODO wherever you left a gap
    • style.md: your voice, sign-offs and banned words
    • rotation.md: twelve monthly themes from your topics
    • sources.md: where the news comes from
    • feedback.md: empty until your first edit
    • weekly-task.md: the instructions the schedule runs

    Fix any TODO now. The drafts are only as good as this folder.

  4. 4
    Read Your First Draft

    Before any schedule exists, it drafts this week's issue so you can judge it. You get a file in drafts/ with:

    • three subject lines and a preheader
    • the email: a hook from this week's news, the month's theme, one thing to do this week, and a reply question
    • the WhatsApp twin, with its character count
    • an SMS twin only if something is time-critical
    • every news item with its link

    There's also an HTML version ready for Beehiiv.

  5. 5
    Give Feedback and Let It Learn

    Reply in the same session in plain words: "Too long; cut the second news item; open with the mistake, not the news." It revises the draft and adds one line per lesson to feedback.md. Every future draft reads that file first, so the second week needs fewer edits than the first.

  6. 6
    Find the Weekly Task Under Routines

    If you said yes to installing the schedule, the desktop app now has a Weekly local task. In the Code tab, click Routines in the sidebar and open it. From its page you can:

    • Run now
    • switch Status between Active and Paused
    • Edit the day, time or instructions
    • Review history

    Each run appears as a new session under Scheduled in the sidebar, with a desktop notification.

    Click Run now once and choose "always allow" for the web search and file tools it asks for, so future runs don't stall waiting for you.

    Tip Tasks only run while the app is open and the computer is awake. Turn on Keep computer awake under Settings → Desktop app → General. A missed run catches up once when the computer wakes.

    Capture Needed

    Claude desktop app → Code tab → Routines → the weekly-letter task's detail page (Run now, Status, Edit, Review history).

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  7. 7
    Paste Into Beehiiv and Schedule It

    When you're happy, open Beehiiv, start a new post and paste the draft's HTML into the editor. Use the subject line you chose and the preheader. Then go to Review → Schedule → Schedule for later, pick your send slot and confirm. Say "sent" in the session, and the draft moves to sent/ so next week's issue builds on it.

  8. 8
    Optional: Let It Create the Beehiiv Draft

    On Beehiiv's Max and Enterprise plans, the Create Post API can put the draft straight into Beehiiv. Create an API key under Settings → Workspace Settings → API (you need to be an owner or admin), save it in the folder's .env file (never in the chat), and say "push". It creates the post as a draft. You still review it and schedule it yourself. On other plans, keep pasting: it takes a minute.

Set Up My AI Newsletter
You are setting up my AI newsletter. Do everything below in this folder, then stop and show me the first draft.

MY INPUTS
- Newsletter name: <name>
- Send slot: <day and time, with timezone>, e.g. Tuesday 09:00 America/New_York
- Draft day: one or two days before the send slot, e.g. Sunday 17:00
- Topics I own (3–5): <topics>
- News sources I trust (3): <sources: sites, newsletters, vendors' changelogs>
- Where the letter lives: Beehiiv
- My Beehiiv plan has the Create Post API (Max or Enterprise): <yes | no>
- Install the weekly schedule now: <yes | no>
- My survey answers (Day 1 and Day 2, pasted from the survey's Copy answers button):
<paste>
- One past email I liked (optional, for the voice):
<paste or "none">

1 · BUILD THE FOLDER
Create newsletter/ with:
- context/offer.md, context/audience.md, context/positioning.md, context/mechanism.md: each written ONLY from my survey answers (who I sell to and who signs, the objection, my offer sentence and offer block, my brand voice, my mechanism and its steps, my strongest proof, my chosen conversion mechanism). Quote my words; invent nothing. Mark anything missing as TODO.
- style.md: my voice (my three adjectives and my three "nots"), sentence length, sign-offs to rotate ("Stay tuned", "Stay curious, stay inspired", "Let's make waves", or ones that fit my voice), banned words (hype, "webinar" if I sell a workshop), and the rule "never state a number or a news fact without a link".
- rotation.md: the 12-month topic rotation. One theme per month, six kinds of theme run twice a year: the problem restated · my mechanism, one step · a customer story · a common mistake · a tool or template · an invitation back in. Fill each month with a theme from MY topics. Mark which month we're in now.
- sources.md: my three sources plus the search queries you'll use each week.
- feedback.md: empty, with a heading "Lessons from my edits".
- drafts/ and sent/ (empty).
- weekly-task.md: the weekly instructions (step 3 below), written out in full so the task is self-contained.

2 · WRITE THE FIRST DRAFT NOW
Follow weekly-task.md once, right now, so I can see a real draft before any schedule exists.

3 · THE WEEKLY TASK (write this into weekly-task.md)
Every week:
a. Read context/, style.md, rotation.md, feedback.md and the last 4 files in sent/.
b. Find this week's news: search the web and my sources for the last 7 days on my topics. Keep the 3 items that matter most to MY audience. Record title, date and link for each. Skip anything you can't link.
c. Pick this month's theme from rotation.md. The letter goes one level deeper on it than last week's issue in sent/.
d. Draft into drafts/<YYYY-MM-DD>.md:
   - 3 subject lines + 1 preheader
   - the email (350–600 words): a hook from this week's news → the theme → one thing to do this week → a reply question; one call to action only if this month's theme is "an invitation back in"
   - a WhatsApp twin under 400 characters (POINTER if the email is over 250 words, otherwise COMPRESSED), with its character count
   - an SMS twin ONLY if something is time-critical this week (one segment: 160 plain GSM-7 characters, no emoji), with its character count; otherwise write "No SMS this week"
   - Sources: every news item with its link
   Also write drafts/<YYYY-MM-DD>.html: the email body as clean HTML for pasting into Beehiiv.
e. Check the draft against style.md and feedback.md before finishing. List any claim without a link and remove it.
f. End with a 3-line summary: the theme, the subject you'd pick, and what you'd like my feedback on.
g. Never publish, send or schedule anything. I approve every issue.
h. When I reply with feedback in this session: revise the draft, then append one line per lesson to feedback.md ("- <date>: <what to do differently next time>").
i. When I say "sent", move the final draft to sent/. If my Beehiiv plan has the Create Post API and I say "push", create the post as a DRAFT through the API using the key in .env (never print it); otherwise tell me to paste the HTML into the Beehiiv editor.

4 · SCHEDULE IT (only if I said yes above)
- If you can create scheduled tasks here (the Claude desktop app): create a WEEKLY local scheduled task named "weekly-letter" on my draft day and time, with this folder as its working folder and the contents of weekly-task.md as its instructions.
- Otherwise (Claude Code in a terminal): write run-weekly.sh that runs `claude -p "$(cat weekly-task.md)"` in this folder and saves the output to drafts/<date>-run.log. Then install it as a weekly launchd job on my draft day and time (a cron line on Linux), and show me how to check it and how to remove it.
Then tell me exactly where to find the task and how to run it now.

Day 3Launch the AI RevOps Engine · Test It, Then Grow It

Make an AI Run the Whole Thing — Then Prove It Works

Today the funnel stops being a stack of files and becomes a living system: built by an agent, instrumented end to end, wired into a CRM and a set of automations, and then pointed at a small amount of real traffic to find out whether any of it is true.

We'll use Claude Code as the worked example throughout. The system is AI-agnostic — the same context and the same prompts work in any agentic coding tool. What matters is the ritual, not the vendor.

Step 1 — The Build Ritual

Here's the deal: the difference between an AI that builds you a funnel and an AI that builds you a generic template is what you give it before you ask. Handing an agent "build me a funnel" gets you a template. Handing it your conversion engine, your spec outline and a build checklist gets you your funnel.

Eight phases — and the agent refuses to skip ahead
Phase 3 is the whole trick. An agent that restates your spec before building gives you one cheap chance to catch a misunderstanding. An agent that starts coding immediately gives you an expensive one, later.
◆ Do this · make the agent interview you

Your first message should forbid code. Load the context, then say: "Read these in full. Confirm you've read them. Then interview me — brand and story, the diagnostic, offer and pricing, traffic channels, tech and deploy target — a few questions at a time, and wait for my answers. Restate the complete spec for my approval. Do not write any code until I approve it."

It feels slower. It is dramatically faster, because you are not debugging a funnel built on a guess.

Task 4.1Run the Ritual End to End
  1. Put your Day-2 engine, your spec outline and your Day-3 asset list in one folder.
  2. Open your agent in that folder so it can read them.
  3. Send the no-code-yet prompt. Answer the interview honestly — "I don't know yet" is a valid answer and better than a made-up one.
  4. Read the spec it restates. Actually read it. This is the cheapest review you will ever do.
  5. Approve, then let it build, showing you each stage as it lands.
OwnerYou · agent buildsToolClaude Code, or any agentic toolTime3–5 hDeliverableA live URL and a spec file you can editProofYou change a price in the spec and the live page updates

What the Orchestrator Actually Is

Once it's built, the agent doesn't go away. It keeps the context — your offer, your ICP, your pages, your templates, your numbers — and becomes the thing you and your team ask questions of and give instructions to.

The RevOps orchestrator — context in, operations out
The retention unlock: a central orchestrator that holds all your funnel knowledge is what turns a pile of files into a system anyone on the team can query instantly.
◆ The real unlock — most people get this wrong

The biggest problem isn't making the orchestrator "perfect." You can refine that forever. The real problem is instant access to every piece of knowledge in your funnel. When anyone on your team can ask "what's our offer for cold LinkedIn leads?" and get an answer in two seconds, that speed becomes a retention advantage. Knowledge you can reach beats knowledge you merely have.

Step 2 — Instrument Every Step, or the Second Half of Today Does Not Work

This is the part people skip, and it's the part that decides whether you have a funnel you can improve or a funnel you can only rebuild. Every step fires one event. The count of that event is the metric. A rate is one count divided by another.

#EventFires whenWhere the count comes from
1sessionthe entry page loadsAnalytics + your own event store
2startfirst interaction — first field, first question, first playAnalytics + event store
3qualify_completethe qualification questions are answeredAnalytics + event store
4step_answereach individual question or milestone — carries its own idEvent store + session recording
5engage_completethey finish the main body — the assessment, the session, Part 1Analytics + event store
6goals_completegoals and history capturedAnalytics + event store
7result_viewthe personalised result or offer reveal is shownAnalytics + event store
8offer_viewthe pricing or plan screen is shownAnalytics + event store
9checkout_startcheckout opensAnalytics + payment provider
10purchasethe charge succeeds — confirmed server-sidePayment API + CRM
11upsell_takean add-on is acceptedPayment API + CRM
Two destinations, always. Send every event to your analytics platform and to a first-party endpoint you control. Analytics gives you the exploration tools; your own store means you still have the data when a platform changes its API, its retention window, or its price.
◆ Pro tip · event number 4 is the one that pays for itself

Per-question and per-milestone drop-off is how you find out that question seven is costing you a fifth of your completions. Aggregate completion rate tells you something is wrong. Per-step drop-off tells you exactly what to delete.

Task 4.2Fire All Eleven, Then Prove They Arrive

Instrument, then verify — the verification is the task.

  1. Install analytics and a session-recording tool. Both have free tiers; there is no excuse.
  2. Fire every event to both destinations, with the UTM attached so buyers map back to a channel.
  3. Walk the funnel yourself, end to end, on a phone, and watch the events land in real time.
  4. Confirm each one is queryable through an API — not just visible in a dashboard. If an agent can't fetch it headlessly, your weekly loop will be manual forever.
OwnerYou · agent wires itToolAnalytics · recordings · your event endpointTime2–3 hDeliverable11 events live, queryable by APIProofOne real session produces all 11 in order

Step 3 — Wire the Pipeline

Events tell you what happened on a page. The pipeline tells you what happened to a person. You need both, and the pipeline is what makes forecasting possible.

Eleven stages, two exits, and the automation that guards each one

Step 4 — The Eight Automations

These are the eight a webinar needs (an RSP and a challenge shift the count; see below), and they carry the load. Each is a trigger, a condition and an action — and each one replaces a thing a human would otherwise forget to do.

Trigger → condition → action, eight times
Automations 1–6 are event-driven and fire instantly. 7 and 8 are polled, because inboxes and clocks don't send webhooks — and the polling interval is a cost decision, not a technical one.
Build them in this order. 1, 3 and 4 are the minimum viable set — confirm, capture, and tag. Everything else is leverage you add once the first three are provably reliable.
Task 4.3Wire the Pipeline and the First Three Automations

Don't try to build all eight today. Build the three that stop you losing data, and test each one with a real contact before moving on.

  • Custom fields first — source, UTM, the four tags, score and band. Adding a field later means back-filling every contact you've already captured.
  • Then the pipeline stages, with the trigger for each transition written down next to it. A stage with no trigger is a stage you'll be updating by hand.
  • Then automations 1, 3 and 4. Register yourself. Attend. Then register again and deliberately no-show. Confirm the tags land correctly both times.
OwnerYou · agent wires itToolYour CRM + automation toolTime4–6 hDeliverablePipeline + fields + 3 live automationsProofA deliberate no-show gets the no-show tag without you touching anything
◆ What changes per funnel type · the automations
Webinar FunnelAll eight apply as written. Automation 8 is the heaviest lifter — the timed reminder engine is what carries show-up to 89%.
Workshop · ChallengeAdd a ninth: the daily generation loop. Survey submitted → agent generates the day's output → PDF and link delivered. It runs once a day, three days running, and it is the product.
Reverse SqueezeAutomation 8 disappears entirely — there's no clock. It's replaced by depth-threshold triggers, which fire per person rather than per schedule.
Other types: tripwire and free-plus-shipping funnels need a fulfilment trigger on purchase · product launches need a hard cart-close job that actually disables checkout · JV funnels need attribution and payout splitting at the moment of sale, because reconciling it later is how partnerships end.

Step 5 — Point Real Traffic at It

Everything up to now is a hypothesis. The only thing that turns it into knowledge is strangers. Today you run a deliberately small test — small enough that being wrong is cheap, big enough that the result isn't noise.

The test campaign — what to spend, what to watch, what it means
The point of today's traffic is not sales. It's to find out which of yesterday's assumptions was wrong, while being wrong is still cheap.
Task 4.4Run the Test and Write Down What Broke
  1. QA first. Every page at 375, 768 and 1280px. A real purchase. Every event firing. Do not send traffic to a funnel you haven't walked yourself.
  2. Launch the smallest version of each live channel, all UTM-tagged, all pointing at one URL.
  3. Wait. Reading numbers after four hours is how people kill things that were working.
  4. Pull both reports and find the single worst step. Not the worst three. The worst one.
  5. Write down what surprised you. That sentence is the most valuable output of the entire day.
OwnerYouToolYour channels + both reportsTime2 h to launch, then waitDeliverableLive traffic, both reports, one named bottleneckProofEvery buyer traces back to a channel via their UTM
◆ Your Day 3 output — half one

A live funnel at a real URL, built from a spec you can edit, with all eleven events firing to two destinations, a pipeline that updates itself, the three critical automations running, real traffic flowing through it, and both reports assembled — plus one named bottleneck to attack tomorrow.

◆ Tonight's homework · 20 minutes

Let the traffic run overnight. Don't touch anything. Tomorrow is about reading what it tells you and deciding what to change — and you cannot read a signal you keep interrupting.

Half two · grow it

Read the Numbers, Fix the Worst One, Repeat

You have a funnel and you have data. This half is the discipline that turns those into a business: know your unit economics, find the single worst step, change one thing, measure, keep or revert. Every week, forever.

◆ Why one leak at a time

Fixing five things at once feels productive and teaches you nothing — if the number moves you can't say which change did it, and if it drops you can't say which to undo. One change per leak is slower per week and vastly faster per quarter.

Step 1 — Know What a Customer Costs and What They're Worth

Two numbers decide whether you have a business or an expensive hobby: what it costs to acquire a customer, and what that customer is worth over their life. If the second is comfortably bigger than the first, you can buy growth. If it isn't, more traffic just loses money faster.
